66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary:
Idaho carries the country's strictest criminalised restroom regime. Its 2026 facility-use law, effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching their birth sex — in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants and hospitals — with a misdemeanour of up to one year and a felony of up to five years on a repeat within five years. Four successive legislative rounds ran from 2023 to 2026, alongside a ban on official recognition of Pride flags.

A federal lawsuit followed the law's passage; contemporaneous reporting states the law was partially blocked, leaving it in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Since then a March 2026 bill extending felony restroom penalties to all public accommodations has passed the House, a March 2026 forced-outting statute has been signed, a birth-marker freeze has been in effect since January 2026, and the federation's Supreme Court declined in 2024 to review the state's bar on gender-affirming care.

The ACLU filed suit on 30 April 2026 arguing due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations, noting the law targets no actual criminal conduct.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary:
Louisiana posts the country's highest measured killing rate against trans women: 24.7 per 100k trans women per year reported, 11.6 recorded, on the TGEU trans-murder-monitoring base (428 US victims, 2008–2025) — a floor rather than a total, though the same analysis cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and the top-ranked state records 23.5. In custody, a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence was killed by other inmates at Angola prison on 2 April 2024, at least the 16th violent death of a trans or gender-expansive person that year; killings continued into 2026.

On 31 May 2026 a mob of about ten beat a trans couple, Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders, outside a women's restroom at a park in Benton; no attacker was arrested, while both victims were charged with disturbing the peace and Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a female marker on her licence. On 15 July 2026 the Bossier Parish Police Jury unanimously approved — on the first of two required votes, reportedly at the sheriff's request — a local ordinance criminalising trans restroom use, described as one of the most punitive in the country. Louisiana has no statewide adult bathroom ban, so the parish ordinance is the state's sharpest instrument.

66186276B29106115751815.name: Texas
66186276B29106115751815.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary:
Tennessee is the only state in the country with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere a child could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable and current: the appeals court revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure today rather than a dead-letter law.

For practical safety, killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

Stat. 553.865) makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; the ACLU of Florida calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 states with facility restrictions only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself.

In March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban. A Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.

Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts Florida's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law states — itself an undercount floor.

sources.title: Missouri Ends Gender-Affirming Care for Transgender Inmates

66186276B75419826371250.summary:
A July 2026 national data analysis places Georgia’s recorded killing rate for trans women at 4.8 per 100k per year — among the country’s highest — and a state law-review article documents a long-run fatality concentration around the city of Atlanta: at least 15 fatal cases statewide across 1990–2014 (11 in Atlanta) and 16 more across 2015–2023 (8 in Atlanta), both series treated by their authors as undercount floors; the analysis’s warning is that a legal-risk grade describes how the state behaves, not how its people do, and Georgia’s documented danger to trans people has been violence on the street more than legislation from the legislature.

On the legal side, licensed medical professionals may not provide patients under 18 with hormone therapy or surgery related to gender transition — the law has applied since 1 July 2023, licence revocation is a possible penalty, and minors who began hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue — and adult gender-affirming surgery access has shrunk: a medical centre in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on 13 February 2025 citing state and national law.

sources.title: Georgia agrees to pay for gender-affirming care for public employees

sources.summary: Wikipedia's state page for Nevada records that the state's anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, and that since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required and similar changes available for driver's licenses and state IDs; a May 2017 law (signed June 22, 2017) abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents. In March 2018 the state's Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex-reassignment surgery costs, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and Nevada offers an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licenses, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required (2019). In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, while the legislature-passed 2023 omnibus bill SB 302 shielding gender-affirming care and abortion was vetoed by the governor; a separate June 2023 bill requiring health insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments became law effective January 1, 2024. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth.

sources.title: Colorado Supreme Court sides with transgender youth in fight against Children's Hospital Colorado
sources.summary: The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on May 18, 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated the state's anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume the care (puberty blockers, hormone therapy). Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision 'denies petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity'; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system. The ruling documents Colorado's highest court actively enforcing the gender-identity protections on which this record's anti-discrimination claim rests.

sources.title: Colorado voters will decide whether to ban trans kids from gendered sports, outlaw gender-affirming surgery for children
sources.summary: Colorado voters will decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender kids from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after state elections officials certified the voter signatures on the three measures including Initiative 108 on child sex trafficking (The Colorado Sun, Mar. 17, 2026). The initiatives were pushed by conservative activists and would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into state law. They are the first statewide ballot-level counter-pressure to Colorado's protective legal posture that this record documents.

sources.title: Colorado to suspend Medicaid coverage for some gender-affirming care for youth due to new federal rule
sources.summary: Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning Oct. 13, 2026, because a new federal rule finalized in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care for people under 18 (and under 19 under the CHP+ child program); the state's Medicaid agency said resuming coverage 'will require legislative action' (The Colorado Sun, Aug. 21, 2026). About 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, and patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period while behavioural healthcare is unaffected. The suspension shows Colorado's protections operating under direct federal-funding pressure, relevant to a trans visitor's assessment of the state.

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
The region contains two of the six regions with the highest recorded counts of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence in the 2012-2025 region-by-region study maintained by the country's principal LGBT monitoring project.

Against that stands the strongest judicial response to transphobic violence recorded anywhere in the country: in January 2025 a first-instance court in this region's main university city recognised a "transphobic motive" in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the association that supports trans sex workers, and - for the first time - admitted the national trans-movement organisation as civil party.

For a visitor the combination is specific: the highest-frequency regions of the country's violence record are here, but so is a documented court that named transphobic motive and ordered reparation.

Provides the per-region violence distribution used to score all Italian units.

sources.title: Era giusto rimuovere i manifesti di Pro Vita, i giudici danno ragione al Comune di Roma
sources.summary: On August 30, 2025 Rome's municipal administration announced that the Consiglio di Stato (the country's highest administrative court, seated in Rome) had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking 'gender' ideology in schools, on the ground that the images — one showing a boy being given a red hairbow — were discriminatory and that public spaces may not be used for messages that 'generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance', particularly concerning minors. The anti-trans campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The ruling is a dated judicial outcome in the region's largest city confirming that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted there, an institutional datapoint for this region record, which otherwise centres on violence statistics and the transphobic-motive verdict in Perugia.

sources.title: Morte di Samuele De Paoli, la Cassazione conferma l'assoluzione della trans Patrizia
sources.summary: On March 5, 2026 the Court of Cassation confirmed the appeal-court acquittal of trans woman Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson ('Patrizia') over the April 27, 2021 death of Samuele De Paoli in Perugia, finding the death was caused by cardiac arrhythmia from accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the charge of homicide final. The case, in this region's main university city, was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant. For this record it documents that the region's courts and the highest ordinary court decided a high-profile trans-related case on the facts, complementing the record's claim about judicial responses to transphobic violence.

72843720B99597932318450.name: Nord-Ovest
72843720B99597932318450.summary:
This region hosts the country's first and second practical civic gender-recognition schemes: Milano's "registro di genere" - chosen name on civic and municipal documents, public-transport subscriptions and staff badges, created by a 2022 council motion brought by the country's first elected transgender councillor - and Torino's analogous "Identita Alias" practice at the municipality and the public libraries. 82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
In December 2024 this province enacted a package of three laws affecting transgender people as a class: school rules requiring parental notification and consent before staff use a student's gender-related chosen name or pronouns; a prohibition on puberty blockers and hormone therapy for minors; and related vital-statistics amendments. Trans and intersex advocacy organisations said at the time they would continue legal action.

In December 2025 the government invoked the constitutional override clause to shield all three laws from judicial remedy. Two national 2SLGBTQ+ organisations, together with five gender-diverse young people, say the constitutional challenge continues despite the shield - a provincial posture of legislating trans-targeting rules and then placing them beyond the courts.

Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory.

82249235B71336988791422.name: Saskatchewan
82249235B71336988791422.summary:
In August 2023 the provincial government announced school policies requiring parents to be asked for permission before staff use a student's preferred name or pronouns (for pupils under 16), parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs to be paused. The province's senior trial court struck the rule down as unconstitutional; the government responded by legislating the consent rule into the Education Act and invoking the notwithstanding clause to immunise it from judicial review.

The matter went to the province's Court of Appeal, which largely allowed the government's appeal in August 2025; a current-status verification found no later ruling, leaving the re-legislated, shielded policy standing. For a visitor the education rule is primarily resident-facing; the durable signal is institutional: a provincial government re-legislating a policy a court had voided and shielding that from rights review - official hostility hardened past ordinary litigation.

The release that started the court challenge.

Saskatchewan (Minister of Education) v UR Pride Centre, 2025 SKCA 74 (11 Aug 2025): the Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision — courts lack jurisdiction to test s.1/s.15 Charter breaches of the school pronoun-notice policy where s.33 was invoked — so the policy stands. Supersedes the injunction-era chambers ruling.

sources.title: Saskatchewan Appeal Court says challenge of province's pronoun law can continue
sources.summary: The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal ruled Aug. 11, 2025 on the provincial government's appeal in the challenge to the school pronoun law, granting the government's appeal in part but holding that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits Charter rights, and that (LGBTQ+ group) UR Pride's litigation may continue in the Court of King's Bench. The 2023 law requires parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school, and the government had argued its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. Egale Canada co-counsel Bennett Jensen said UR Pride will continue the litigation, noting students had been 'living under the reality of this law' for two years. This mainstream coverage independently traces the record's claim that the appeal court largely allowed the government's appeal while keeping the merits challenge alive.

sources.title: Amnesty International Canada welcomes ruling in court challenge to Saskatchewan pronoun law
sources.summary: Amnesty International Canada welcomed the Aug. 11, 2025 decision of the Court of Appeal for Saskatchewan as a 'meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in Canada', saying courts can still determine whether the province's anti-trans pronoun law violates the Charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down. Amnesty participated as an intervenor in the appeal, arguing that use of the clause must align with Canada's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy. The piece corroborates the durable signal this record draws from the case: a consent and name-change rule for transgender pupils shielded from ordinary rights review while litigation continues.

sources.title: Supreme Court to weigh in on Saskatchewan's school pronoun case
sources.summary: On Nov. 6, 2025 the Supreme Court of Canada said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to Saskatchewan's school pronoun law, which since 2023 has required parental consent before children under 16 change their names or pronouns at school and has been shielded by the province's invocation of the Charter's notwithstanding clause (a five-year override). Both the province and LGBTQ+ group UR Pride appealed the Court of Appeal decision that the challenge can continue, and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to Quebec's Bill 21. The grant is the key later development for this record: no merits ruling has changed the policy, but the constitutionality of the re-legislated, shielded consent rule is now before Canada's highest court.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for the informal use of chosen names and pronouns by students of any age (it remains required for formal use in official records for students under 16), with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its application to the whole school environment, including "visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors", so current school rules technically reach non-residents present in classrooms.

Deviation: 0.02 below the national score of 0.86. The reversal is a strong positive institutional response — a government that legislated against trans students repealed the provision after one term. The residual signal is the demonstrated capacity for hostile policy within an election cycle and the 2023 protest period, which create a slightly higher baseline of political volatility than provinces that never legislated against trans people. No street-level disruption of public expression events was documented.

Compared to Alberta (0.76) and Saskatchewan (0.79), New Brunswick is materially higher: it did not use the notwithstanding clause, and its hostile policy was reversed rather than immunised from judicial review. Compared to the national score, the gap is small and time-sensitive — the current effective policy is protective, and further reversal would bring New Brunswick to or above the national level.

Its application clause covers the school environment including all students plus "school personnel, contract/casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors" — the school-environment rules therefore reach non-residents present in classrooms.

sources.title: Policy 713: LGBT school policy change causes political turmoil in Canada
sources.summary: On 1 July 2023, changes to New Brunswick's Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity policy (Policy 713) took effect, barring teachers from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent and dropping explicit wording that let students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. Premier Blaine Higgs's Progressive Conservative government updated the policy without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers, and two ministers quit in protest while two others were pushed out. Party dissidents called for a leadership review and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick 'need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians'. Documents the July 2023 amendment and political crisis this record describes.

Eight Progressive Conservative members, including six cabinet ministers, sat out question period to protest the lack of process and transparency, and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said trans kids in New Brunswick 'need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians'. sources.title: 'We know it saves lives:' hundreds go to N.B. rally against review of LGBTQ policy
sources.summary: About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the government's review of Policy 713, the 2020 policy that requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and provide gender-neutral bathrooms. Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write the policy, said 'we know it saves lives' and warned that 'with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids', while Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review. Documents the public protest against the Higgs government's move to amend the sexual-orientation and gender-identity policy this record is about.

14339913B23556801435424.name: Scotland
14339913B23556801435424.summary:
This region's prosecution system names anti-trans crime as its own charging category: the region's 2021 hate-crime statute created a dedicated transgender-identity aggravation, and the prosecuting authority reported 104 charges carrying it in 2025-26 (up 21% on 86 the year before), while police recorded 8,538 hate crimes in the provision's first full year. For a visitor who is assaulted or harassed, the machinery exists to see the offence counted and charged by name.

The region's parliament passed a more expansive self-declaration gender-recognition law with a two-thirds majority in December 2022 - evidence of markedly more trans-accepting regional institutions; the same nation-wide rules on legal sex and single-sex services apply here as across the parent nation.

31927357B79016588373767.summary:
The capital recorded the highest transfeminicide toll in the country in 2024 — 17 LGBT+ homicides, of which 11 were trans women — and remains among the highest-count states in 2025. The raw violence data is a negative signal for a visitor, though part of the elevated count reflects the capital's superior reporting infrastructure rather than proportionally higher danger.

Counterbalanced by the strongest institutional response of any Mexican state: transfeminicide was made a distinct crime in July 2024 (“Ley Paola Buenrostro”, the second state to do so); a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit created in December 2024 covers all violent deaths of trans women; a prosecutor's protocol (Acuerdo FGJCDMX/04/2025) requires feminist-context investigation with immediate-action deadlines; and a new Gender Police launched in August 2025 with 30 patrol units. For a visitor assaulted in the capital there is trained machinery to investigate, where other jurisdictions have none. Modestly above the national score (0.55): the protective and investigative framework is the strongest in Mexico and materially changes what a visitor who encounters violence or discrimination faces after the fact, even though the pre-violence risk data is the country's worst.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Three trans women murdered in less than a week in July 2024 (one disappeared and found dead days later; one killed while sex work); four transfeminicides recorded in July 2024 alone and five for the year in the national NGO yearbook — second only to Mexico City. Activists reported six trans women killed in a short period and accused three levels of government of rights omissions. Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and its 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity — meaning a visitor assaulted in Monterrey faces a legal framework with no specific protective category. The state has an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2-5 years, and the national observatory's verdict on such statutes is that transfeminicide 'advances in law but not in sentences.'

Legislative response has been refusal: an initiative filed by Colectivo Casa Trans was 'ignored and finally lapsed,' prompting a 50+-day protest encampment outside the state congress still ongoing in January 2026 (activists report harassment and lack of basic facilities at the camp). A PT deputy in 2026 could only ask the congress to 'unfreeze' the bill. There is no investigative unit, no protocol, and no named offence to invoke. The gap between nominal coverage and protection is documented in the observatory review 'transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.'

Context for comparison: Mexico City pairs a similar lethality record with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit (Dec 2024), mandatory-response protocols and a gender police force (Aug 2025); Nayarit was first in the country to typify the crime (March 2024). Nuevo León's explicit legislative refusal is the opposite signal.

Records CDMX as the state with the most LGBT+ killings in 2024 (17 homicides, 11 trans women) ahead of Nuevo León (5); notes the Mexican state has no official registry of bias-motivated violence, and documents under-counting where media accounts lack victim names and gender data.

Verificado (2024): Nuevo Leon recorded 7 attacks on LGBT people, 3 forced disappearances and 4 transfeminicides during the year, and transfeminicidio is not typified in the state penal code. ABC Noticias (12 Jan 2026): Colectivo Casa Trans has held a planton of more than 50 days outside the Nuevo Leon congress pressing legislators to typify transfeminicidio in the state penal code; their bill was ignored for a year and lapsed, forcing a fresh filing.

31927357B49073316106075.summary:
The state has not typified hate crime at all, per its own LGBT+ welfare sub-director (June 2026), who also located most attacks on the community in Tierra Caliente, the zone of armed-group influence. Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the first four and a half months of 2026 alone, including 'Daniela,' a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026 — a suspect was arrested, a positive institutional response. Two additional deaths in Morelia in April 2026, one of them a gay man, were linked by the attorney general's office to organised crime. An NGO observatory report counted 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024, led by Morelia (11), then Lázaro Cárdenas (6), Apatzingán and Uruapan (5) and Zamora (4), with 2015 the deadliest year (10 victims).

Colectivo PRIDE Michoacán reports rising attacks in the municipalities bordering Jalisco, that victims are no longer attended to, and that the state does not acknowledge the violence. No transfeminicide offence, no hate-crime typification, no investigative protocol — the only counterweights are individual arrests.

Context for comparison: Veracruz, similarly hostile, at least passed a gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025; Mexico City pairs comparable lethality with a dedicated transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocols. Michoacán has no legal machinery whatsoever, plus an armed-group amplifier that makes the violence harder to escape or report.

The record's core practical-safety signal is the worst in the national data: this state led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, with 19 of 32 jurisdictions recording victims — and closed 2025 with at least 15 recorded hate crimes; the killing of a 27-year-old trans woman, stabbed to death in a motel on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted nine hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women, and the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as this state's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform.

Legal protections and enforcement are absent in practice: before the 2025 civil-code gender-identity reform — among the last to be legislated — a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct gender documents, and there is no functioning investigation or prosecution machinery, distinct from other jurisdictions where laws exist but enforcement is weak. Activists cite deliberate filing-away of cases, the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely, and in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the homicide file had simply disappeared; the impunity here is total.

The report notes under-reporting: in a third of 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex recorded was male without attention to gender identity.

State ranking: Puebla 7, then Veracruz and Guanajuato 6 each; includes a Veracruz case (Oluta motel killing, Nov 2025).

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body, and the events are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.

Newer reporting profiles the region as a fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, with possible municipal-police participation, and the official answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. A trans visitor therefore stands under a formally protective framework alongside customary exclusion and violent-incident reports at exactly the events tourists attend.

Three velas went ahead on 26 May, with muxes affirming they are part of local society and culture.

State response has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform.

31927357B1137737933275.name: Puebla
31927357B1137737933275.summary: Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people, and trans women were 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year across at least 17 states reporting victims - a top-of-table lethality record a visitor must weigh against any formal protections. Its legal gender recognition law (2021) still carries an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, and the state congress has still not corrected the text: for a visitor whose documents must match their presentation, the unmet duty to conform the law to the binding ruling is itself a live hostility signal, and no state-level enforcement data exists to temper it.

1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 people crossing the long, porous international border - including seven transgender people - in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to the financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power. On the audited record there is no statute criminalising trans presence here; the documented harm is police practice at the checkpoints.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal replicates the checkpoint script documented in its neighbour: police arrested a transgender person arriving from across the long, porous international border for allegedly "infiltrating", treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity. It is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating that some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime occurs at a detectable rate.

The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than a repeated-sweep pattern elsewhere: the documented record here is a single arrest plus the broader infiltration framing. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism - trans presentation treated as evidence of illegal entry.

sources.title: The Reality of Transgender Welfare Boards in India: An RTI Investigation
sources.summary: The Quint (5 November 2024) publishes an RTI investigation into transgender welfare boards: West Bengal is one of the 12 states/UTs that notified a board, but the majority of boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since their creation, and the 17 existing boards 'are mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism, or any power', with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people. Supports this record's claim that West Bengal's constituted welfare board operates without a functioning policy framework.

sources.title: Transwoman alleges RPF constable groped her to 'check gender'
sources.summary: Times of India, Kolkata (18 August 2024): a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR alleging an RPF constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them 'to check her gender' and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears. Documents the state-actor gender-checking conduct this record associates with West Bengal's policing of trans people.

sources.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia on India's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab: it was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people, though the page records criticism that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. This protective national framework is the statute a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under and supports the record's statement that no statute in Punjab targets trans people.

14911670B91095571793858.summary:
The risk signal for this jurisdiction is a violence-rate spike: zero recorded trans killings in 2024 jumped to 4 in 2025 — the sharpest deterioration in the dataset. Against a population of ~3.5 million, four cases yield approximately 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and roughly three times the national figure of ~0.38/million. The dataset cautions against reading a single-year zero as safety and notes the volatility.

For a visitor, the small absolute numbers mean a single incident dramatically shifts perception, and the volatility suggests the environment can turn rapidly. No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies; the risk is purely a violence-rate signal.

14911670B85657526756793.name: Rio de Jeneiro
14911670B85657526756793.summary:
Rio de Janeiro recorded only 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — roughly 0.18 per million against a population near 17 million — well below the national average, so lethal violence is the weakest part of the risk picture here. The visitor-facing signals are about enforcement: a documented extortion racket in Niterói ran for about two years under the appearance of backing from public agents, and in Copacabana the tourist police arrested two trans women for extorting a visiting tourist with threats to circulate intimate videos.

Institutional response was mixed. The state court decreed preventive detention in February 2026 for the alleged extorter, an ex-employee of Niterói city hall, so the judiciary can act, and the tourist-police arrests likewise show police presence in tourist areas. Yet the Niterói scheme operated openly for roughly two years, forcing trans sex workers to pay weekly exactions, which signals weak protection for the most exposed trans residents and a tourist-area climate in which visibly trans people may be treated as scam suspects.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025 — about 0.83 per million per year, more than double the national rate — after the 2024 dossier counted 8 killings in the state, its highest year. The dossier's finding that most killings happen outside the capitals makes small-town exposure relevant for visitors travelling beyond the capital, so the elevated per-capita reading is the core of the assessment even though three cases on a small population are statistically fragile.

On documents and institutional response, two local positives exist: a 2021 decree guarantees the social-name right, accepted by state public offices and usable on badges, cards and identification documents, and a 2026 jury conviction of 13 years and 6 months for the gender-motivated killing of a trans woman shows the courts can deliver. No trans-specific ordinance or protection beyond these was found; the national framework applies uniformly.

10402087B89016843004490.name: Sachsen
10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Two documented 2025 features raise Sachsen above the German norm for visitor risk around queer visibility: neo-Nazis mounted a counter-protest intended to disrupt Dresden's pride march on 31 May 2025 (the march proceeded); and the state government, with two neighbouring states, co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act after an abuse-of-self-ID court case ('Fall Liebich'), alleging misuse of the self-ID right — an organised, multi-state push to roll back trans self-determination law.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
The Comunitat Valenciana holds both a dedicated integral law on the right to gender identity and expression and a general LGTBI-equality statute — one of only three communities to legislate in both the trans-specific and general-LGTBI categories — and, unlike the peer community that shares the dual structure, it has not amended or narrowed its provisions. The statutory framework supports institutional response channels for a visitor encountering discrimination.

Enforcement evidence is thin but positive: a documented conviction in the community's court system — six months' prison, suspended, plus fines and a moral-damages payment — for chasing, insulting and recording a trans woman solely because of her gender identity shows the institutional response channel for discrimination operates. No negative visitor-facing finding, incident pattern or enforcement gap was located in the research pass, and the capital carries a visible, well-established LGTBI community with dedicated infrastructure.

sources.summary: Spanish trans-rights platform's inventory of autonomous-community gender-identity laws, listing Comunitat Valenciana with two statutes: Ley 8/2017 of 7 April (integral recognition of the right to gender identity and expression) and Ley 23/2018 of 29 November (LGTBI equality) — the two-statute combination the record's framework claim rests on. Neighbouring communities listed for contrast carry only single statutes (e.g. Cataluña Ley 11/2014, Aragón Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spanish regions: tracks which autonomidades have gender-identity protocols and education legislation; notes the Valencian parliament completing its gender legislation and groups the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage.

sources.title: BOE-A-2017-5118 Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresión de género en la Comunitat Valenciana. - BOE
sources.summary: Official gazette text of the Comunitat Valenciana's Ley 8/2017, de 7 de abril, integral del reconocimiento del derecho a la identidad y a la expresion de genero, published as BOE-A-2017-5118. Article 1 makes the law's purpose the guarantee of an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana must treat people according to their felt gender identity; Title III provides for administrative documentation and an advice-and-support service for trans people and their families. Primary legal text confirming the 'dedicated integral law on the right to identity and gender expression' this record cites, enacted 7 April 2017.

sources.title: BOE-A-2019-281 Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI. - BOE
sources.summary: Official gazette text of Ley 23/2018, de 29 de noviembre, de igualdad de las personas LGTBI (BOE-A-2019-281), the Comunitat Valenciana's general equality statute for LGTBI people. Its provisions cover non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, access and admission rights (art. 56), reversal of the burden of proof (art. 57), and a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions (arts. 58-66) for discrimination against LGTBI people. Primary legal text confirming the community's general-LGTBI-statute category alongside its 2017 trans-specific law, the dual-category statutory framework on which this record's assessment rests.

sources.title: Seis meses de carcel por perseguir, insultar y grabar a una persona trans en Valencia - Observatorio de delitos de odio y discriminacion
sources.summary: Report of a conviction by the Audiencia Provincial de Valencia (Section 5) over a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park (Patraix), where an 18-year-old with several minors insulted, chased, recorded and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. 19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country: the provincial human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police — or by third parties under police cover — against trans and travesti people during operations in three cities (La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría), under 'preventive policing' frameworks. Academic legal analysis confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution — devolved to provincial justice in 2005 — and street-offence law as the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity: a patterned, state-implicated escalation.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is arbitrary detention during any police stop. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework that measurably increased police persecution of trans women, and the protective institutions that coexist — the provincial ombudsman's 2024 registry-rectification guide and its discrimination-caseload machinery — are resident-facing and do not offset that exposure. No provincial law criminalises gender identity; enforcement practice, not statute, does the work.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
For a trans traveler the exposure here is social rather than statutory: the local anti-LGBT declarations were never criminal statutes, and every such document in the country had been repealed or invalidated by 24 April 2025, when the county charter that was the country's final surviving holdout was repealed at an extraordinary session; this state/province's own resolution had been repealed on 20 September 2021.

Practical safety is the operative concern: the repeal was forced from outside (the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds) rather than produced by a change in local attitudes, so the de facto social climate that generated the resolutions is assessed to persist. Being visibly trans at a public event in an eastern town whose local authority resisted all external pressure until 2025 carries harassment exposure, and the record shows executive intent to exclude a visible LGBTQ public presence - the capital's mayor banned the 2019 equality march on security grounds, the district court overturned the ban, and the march proceeded.

17162690B23777949290372.name: Podlaskie Voivodeship
17162690B23777949290372.summary:
Podlaskie saw Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event: at the 20 July 2019 Białystok Equality March, roughly 1,000 marchers were attacked by thousands of far-right and football-hooligan groups who attempted to block the route. Police detained 25 people; 32 counter-demonstrations had been registered that day, including a prayer vigil at the Cathedral Basilica. In the run-up, Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda had a proclamation read in every church across the region. The surrounding Białystok County had been declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, though the city itself did not adopt one, and its mayor questioned whether the march was "needed" while the PiS city council filed a motion to stop it.

The state's protective response improved materially: at the fourth Equality March (28 September 2024), ~300 participants were escorted by 500 police officers and the Podlaskie police reported zero incidents. This is positive evidence under the single-incident rule (institutional learning, proportionate deployment), but it does not erase the 2019 pattern—organised mass violence met with a partial 25-person detention response, embedded in a documented church-and-county mobilisation infrastructure.

Score of 0.44 sits 0.08 below the national 0.52. Slightly above Subcarpathian (0.42), which lacked Podlaskie's demonstrable five-year improvement in state protection, but below Masovian (0.56), where the institutional machinery runs the other way.

Anchors the record's claim of Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event with dates and scale.

17162690B69262761487853.name: Lublin Voivodeship
17162690B69262761487853.summary:
Lubelskie carried a voivodeship-level "LGBT-free" resolution from 2020 until its 20 September 2021 repeal under European Commission funding pressure. Its municipality of Świdnik (population ~40,000) was the first local authority in all of Poland to adopt an anti-LGBT resolution (March 2019, "against homopropaganda, LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of Polish children"), and its deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to Warsaw's LGBT+ Declaration signed a month earlier. Świdnik became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as with other eastern voivodeships the repeal was coerced rather than converted—the underlying civic mobilisation that produced Poland's first-ever anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the voivodeship scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

Score of 0.45 sits 0.07 below the national 0.52. Above Subcarpathian (0.42), which additionally produced a mayoral march ban and held out until 2025, and above Podlaskie (0.44), where the 2019 coordinated mass assault adds a violence dimension absent in Lublin. Below Małopolska (0.48), which pairs its resolution history with Kraków's clearly positive institutional trajectory.

17162690B84565288021286.name: Masovian Voivodeship
17162690B84565288021286.summary:
Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. On 6 February 2024, Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. Warsaw is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (Świdnik, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from Warsaw by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the Supreme Administrative Court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city under mayor Lech Kaczyński banned that year's Parada Równości, and the ECtHR in Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13, and 14 ECHR. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive.

Score of 0.56 sits 0.04 above the national 0.52. The only unit scoring above national in this dossier; well above Małopolska (0.48) and the eastern belt (0.42–0.45), where the resolution legacy dominates and no equivalent court-repeal or declaration infrastructure exists.

27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
For a trans traveler Bauchi means exposure to a religious criminal code with a capital ceiling: the religious penal code of this state/province remains in force (a June 2025 government note confirms it), and its courts are on record as the place where the ultimate penalty was actually pronounced - in June 2022 a religious court in the town of Ningi sentenced three men, including a 70-year-old, to death by stoning for same-sex acts after a religious-police arrest, the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in the country. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out: no execution is on record, the accused were released on bail pending appeal, and the June 2025 note records the sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the governor of this state/province.

Practical safety: the moral code is actively enforced - the same government note places a further death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a religious court in this state/province in May 2024, and advisory material in 2025-26 continues to cite corporal enforcement of religious morality law in this state/province. The appellate counterweight exists but is fragile: an upper court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003, and a monitoring organisation recorded further successful appeals.

27671186B99510750195830.name: Sokoto
27671186B99510750195830.summary:
For a trans traveler Sokoto is a statutory-exposure record with verified court-level enforcement: the religious penal code of this state/province took effect on 31 January 2001; male same-sex activity draws death by stoning for married or previously-married offenders and 100 lashes for the unmarried, while acts between women draw a discretionary sentence of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. A June 2025 government note confirms the code remains in force.

Practical safety: a 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 religious-court cases (2017) covers this state/province among its three sample states/provinces, confirming operational religious courts and religious-police activity here; no capital sentence is on record as imposed in this state/province - that record belongs to a neighbouring state/province - and no trans-specific incident is documented.

sources.summary: Equaldex log entry #14118: the Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect in Sokoto on 31 January 2001; male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and 100 lashes otherwise; sexual acts between women (wsafa) draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment.

sources.title: Proceedings and Judgments in the Safiyatu Hussaini Case (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. V)
sources.summary: This chapter of the academic sourcebook reproduces the full record of a capital prosecution in Sokoto State's Sharia courts. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa (Sokoto State) convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. On her appeal, filed 26 October 2001, the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. For this record the document evidences that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the same capital-punishment framework (for zina, not same-sex conduct) the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

sources.title: Interim and Final Reports of the Committee Set Up to Advise the Sokoto State Government on the Establishment of Sharia (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. II)

They document the state-level groundwork for the Sokoto Sharia Penal Code - in force from 31 January 2001 per this record's other sources - that carries the stoning and lashing penalties for men's same-sex acts described in this record.

27671186B69054806776702.name: Yobe
27671186B69054806776702.summary:
For a trans traveler Yobe is a jurisdiction-level rather than incident-level risk: it is one of twelve states/provinces that extended religious law into criminal jurisdiction during the 1999-2002 wave, giving religious courts authority over Muslims for conduct beyond the national criminal code; a June 2025 government note confirms the religious penal codes remain in force, with death as the maximum penalty for men's same-sex acts across all twelve states/provinces.

Practical safety: the same note's enforcement section records the 2023 public flogging of a person for cross-dressing, a trans-adjacent religious-police punishment, and observes that few cases reach the ordinary courts; national law alone reaches only men's acts, so the parallel religious jurisdiction is the operative exposure here.

27671186B21163522287660.name: Zamfara
27671186B21163522287660.summary:
Zamfara is where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began: its governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 eleven more northern states followed — a parallel system of Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, which the 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms is still operative and capital-punishment-capable for same-sex acts. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 uses Zamfara as one of three sample states, confirming the courts function in practice, not just on paper.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Zamfara, and no trans-specific incident appears in the dossier; the finding is pioneering the bloc's enforcement architecture and hosting functioning religious courts.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

sources.title: On the Adoption and Implementation of Sharia Legal System in Zamfara State (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. II)
sources.summary: Primary state-authored account of Zamfara's Sharia adoption, written by Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, and presented at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. It details Zamfara's enabling legislation - the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999 under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution - which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code, and records the Grand Kadi taking over court administration from 29 June 2000 alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. For this record it documents from inside the state government the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

sources.title: The Making of the Zamfara and Kano State Sharia Penal Codes (Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria, Vol. IV)
sources.summary: Academic reconstruction of how Zamfara's Sharia Penal Code was made: the Zamfara governor appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementing Sharia including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, and by the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia. The chapter analyses the codification of offences and punishments and the penal-code architecture the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, grounding this record's claim that Zamfara pioneered the bloc's religious-criminal framework.

27671186B753479316714.name: Borno
27671186B753479316714.summary:
Borno is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states applying Sharia criminal law in parallel with the federal system since the 1999–2002 wave. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note lists Borno among the states where the Sharia penal code remains in force for Muslims, criminalising same-sex acts between men (death penalty the maximum) and between women (penalties up to flogging and imprisonment), with a dedicated section on enforcement and the religious police — the legal architecture, not a case record, is the finding.

No trans-specific incident, no Hisbah case and no court-level study covers Borno in this dossier; the bloc's own reporting caveat is that enforcement data capture only a fraction of actual cases, so silence is not evidence of safety. The federal criminal code's coverage of men's acts (up to 14 years) applies here as everywhere in Nigeria.

UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria: Islamic law applies to Muslims in the 12 northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all 12 states and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).

sources.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. III, Ch. 3 Part IV — Documentary Materials (Ostien, ed.)
sources.summary: Ostien's Volume III reproduces Borno State's own statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000), gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001 and signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the State; Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'; Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement; and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. Borno's own enacted death penalty for same-gender intercourse independently supports this record's finding that the state's legal architecture, not just the national framework, criminalises same-sex conduct.

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
In Imo, enforcement under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law is active: in February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the law with its 14-year term, expressly framing the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'. The parallel risk is community violence: in April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them, and a follow-up inquiry records that police took the two men into custody.

For a discovered visitor the risk comes from neighbours and police alike: mob justice drew no recorded accountability in 2018, while named command-level enforcement invoked the criminal law in 2025. No visitor documents or border-screening practice, and no marriage or partner-travel provision, is recorded in the dossier for this state.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

sources.summary: On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own — the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) — which criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. The penalty scale runs up to 100 strokes for morality offences, and courts apply it publicly: in August 2025 a Sharia court sitting behind closed doors sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual conduct that carries no criminal penalty in any other province here can be publicly caned by a court in Aceh, so for a visiting couple or a visibly transgender traveller the enforcement exposure is the sharpest documented in the country.

Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens — the academic counterpart to the record's enforcement claims.

65028918B28198720309323.name: Central Kalimantan
65028918B28198720309323.summary:
Central Kalimantan shows no sub-national divergence for a visitor: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is not one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations. Visitor risk therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction.

Ordinary local moral policing seen in some neighbouring provinces is absent here, but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction; any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence, and a transgender visitor should assume the national criminal baseline applies in full.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and that because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline a visitor in Central Kalimantan stands under, consistent with this record's finding that the province's risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
North Sumatra is one of the eight provinces whose regional regulations the national study (OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation) examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, including rules touching sexual orientation and gender expression. No specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted local bylaw targeting transgender people is documented in the dossier, so the signal for a visitor is legal divergence without operational evidence.

Practical reading: the discriminatory-regulations finding is a real but small risk factor absent any enforcement documentation, and the one documented legal-process data point — a local court handling a transgender man's name-change application neutrally over a six-week process, with no enforcement action against the applicant recorded — points to routine if conservative administration rather than active persecution.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: The first but not the last: Indonesian transgender man fights for recognition | UNAIDS
sources.summary: Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan (North Sumatra's capital), described to UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity: after a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application, and the judge, though warning the change would 'erase my identity', stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. For this record it is North Sumatra's only documented legal-process data point: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally and no enforcement action against the couple is recorded anywhere in the article.

sources.title: LGBT Manado Aksi Tolak Kekerasan Seksual - SuaraKita
sources.summary: On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined Manado's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, Manado, from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA; SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation whose director Coco Jericho was quoted, took part. The article records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people - a butch lesbian groped during a raid, per SALUT - and that victims often do not report because of fear their families will not accept their orientation. It documents a public LGBT+ presence in Manado and a local account of raid-era conduct, with no arrests or prosecutions reported in the piece.

sources.title: Ketika Waria Berkontes Ratu Pantai - SuaraKita
sources.summary: On Saturday 10 November (2012) a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach, Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi (BNN) as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS. The report quotes Sinjal saying waria are among local people and deserve attention. It documents official-level engagement with North Sulawesi's waria community through a public pageant - evidence of a visible, organised trans community in Manado - with no adverse official action recorded.

sources.title: Hari Paling Buruk Dalam Hidup Ratu Waria: Media yang Sensasional telah Hancurkan Hidupku - Konde.co
sources.summary: This Konde.co interview profiles Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara 2016-2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado, who says that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. The article confirms a visible trans-women community culture in North Sulawesi - an elected province-level waria queen in Manado - while documenting the media-stoked stigma that follows public visibility. No legal or police action appears anywhere in the account.

65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
Yogyakarta is among the eight provinces whose regional regulations a national study (OutRight's 'Creeping Criminalisation') examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, yet the dossier documents no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people here: the visitor-facing signal is legal divergence without operational evidence.

The one enforcement-adjacent event documented - the February 2016 closure of the trans-Muslim religious school in this special region after a hardline religious group threatened to seal it - proceeded on administrative and religious grounds rather than under any enacted regional anti-trans regulation, and drew public restraint from the regional government. For a traveller, the practical exposure is a discriminatory regulatory layer whose actual operation against visitors is not documented; no trans-specific incident involving travellers, and no visitor documents or border-screening practice, is recorded in the dossier. The national framework therefore carries the assessment, with this region contributing a legal-divergence signal that lacks demonstrated enforcement.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: Pesantren Waria Yogyakarta: Kami hanya belajar agama (BBC Indonesia)
sources.summary: BBC Indonesia (26 February 2016) reports that on the night of Wednesday 24 February 2016 Yogyakarta's Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — a religious school where trans women ('waria') study Islam — was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam (FJI) threatened to seal it, amid what the BBC describes as rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta'. Banguntapan district head (camat) Jati Bayubroto justified the closure on the grounds the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; founder Shinta Ratri said about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. The report documents a concrete, Yogyakarta-located enforcement-adjacent event against a trans institution — the first such incident this record's dossier had recorded — while showing the shutdown proceeded on administrative/religious grounds rather than an enacted regional anti-trans regulation.

sources.title: Pesantren waria di Yogyakarta ditutup sementara (Rappler Indonesia)
sources.summary: Rappler Indonesia's 25 February 2016 report details the closure meeting: on 24 February 2016 at about 20:00 WIB a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta — attended by ward/residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in the earlier 19 February session, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief (Kapolsek) — ended with an agreement to shut the Al-Fatah waria pesantren after the Front Jihad Islam demanded it; a waria witness said an FJI leader delivered 'fiery' anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, calling LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' (fellow children of the nation) and saying the regional government would study the issue. It is the first documented Yogyakarta operational-pressure event for this record's dossier, concluded on administrative/community grounds without any provincial anti-trans statute being cited.

sources.title: Wajah Solidaritas Waria Yogyakarta di Tengah Pandemi (DW Indonesia)
sources.summary: DW Indonesia (21 June 2021) reports that Yogyakarta's trans women ('transpuan'/'waria') — most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic and were, in DW's words, 'ignored by the government', struggling to pay rent and buy food. The article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren in Yogyakarta run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances. It shows the Yogyakarta waria community and pesantren operating again years after the 2016 closure, while documenting persistent economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province.
