76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.

sources.summary: University of KwaZulu-Natal (Durban) Masters criminology thesis, 2024 (Buthelezi, Ayanda Nomfundo): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minority in KwaMashu Township' — 15 queer participants purposively sampled from the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, in-depth interviews; findings report significant victimisation of queer individuals in township settings and examine adequacy of support/interventions and safety strategies.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.

76434192B51294388644125.name: Nothern Cape
76434192B51294388644125.summary:
Three LGBTIQ+ killings were recorded in this province in 2024, two of them suspected hate-crime murders of transgender people: on 14 May 2024 in Upington a 27-year-old transgender woman was stabbed multiple times and her body set on fire in her own room, discovered by a family member who noticed the house burning; on 1 June 2024 an 18-year-old transgender high-school student was stabbed more than 20 times in Kimberley after a man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her on realising she was transgender. A third LGBTIQ+ person - a gay man - was killed in September 2024.

For a traveller, the exposure is severity-weighted: the methods are extreme and the province-level community shock is real, but the incidents are not clearly patterned or state-implicated, and no provincial legislative or enforcement finding against trans visitors is documented. Police opened murder cases in the first two killings - no arrests were reported at the first entry, and a suspect was reportedly arrested in the second (a claim the reporting could not verify with authorities). The register records that police 'identified' the first decedent by a deadname, an institutional practice a visibly trans traveller should anticipate. No visitor documents or border-screening practice is recorded in the dossier.

sources.summary: TGEU Trans Day of Remembrance register entry (14 May 2024): Jo-Ann Isaks, 27, a transgender woman, was found dead in a burning room in the Paballelo location of Upington after multiple stab wounds; a family member noticed the fire at about 23:00. Police (ZF Mgcawu District) confirmed a murder case, with no arrests at the time of the entry, and referred to the decedent by a deadname; the entry quotes district LGBTIQ+ leader Jenny Sambok and reports the province's LGBTIQ+ community 'shaken'.

sources.title: Upington Transgender Woman Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (24 May 2024) reports that on the night of Wednesday 14 May 2024, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was found dead in her burning room in Paballelo township, Upington, after a family member saw flames at about 23:00 and discovered her body — already alight — with multiple stab wounds to the upper body. ZF Mgcawu District Municipality police spokesperson Sgt Omphile Masegela confirmed a murder case had been opened, called the investigation 'at a critical stage', reported no arrests at that date, and police publicly identified the victim as 'Jonathan Isaks' — the deadnaming this record's TGEU entry also recorded. Northern Cape LGBTIQ+ district leader Jenny Sambok said the community in the ZF Mgcawu region had been shaken, providing the local community-level response this dossier cites.

sources.title: Transgender Kimberley High School Teen Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (13 June 2024) reports that on 1 June 2024, 18-year-old transgender learner Karabelo Pudumo — a Grade 10 student at Pescodia High School who lived with her grandparents — was stabbed to death in Kimberley, capital of the Northern Cape; a man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender, stabbing her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, though MambaOnline could not verify this with authorities, and more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. The killing is the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the Northern Cape within a month — after Jo-Ann Isaks' 14 May death in Upington — giving this record's dossier patterning evidence beyond a single incident.

sources.title: Kimberley to Host First-Ever Northern Cape Pride (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (2 November 2024) reports the inaugural Northern Cape Pride, set for 30 November 2024 at Kimberley's Galeshewe Open Air Arena under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', featuring a morning parade, speakers and community activities, with Pride Committee member Tebogo Makwati calling it a historic moment for the province. The article also records that the province saw at least three LGBTIQ+ community members murdered in 2024: Jo-Ann Isaks (27, transgender woman, May), Karabelo Pudumo (18, transgender high school student, June) and a 50-year-old gay man, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas (September). It documents both organised community presence and the year's third and latest killing of an LGBTIQ+ person in the Northern Cape.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.

sources.summary: Published letter (June 2010) from the NHTL and its Provincial Houses after meeting at Hazyview, Mpumalanga: while 'respecting' the Constitutional Court same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'; states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (missing from cache); the underlying 2016 report documents the NHTL asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

sources.title: Murder of lesbian prompts Mpumalanga march against violence (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp (6 January 2020) reports that Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead — half naked with stab wounds — near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, Mpumalanga, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, and that on 2 January about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. The report documents a deadly anti-LGBTIQ incident and local community mobilisation inside Mpumalanga — province-level violence data this record's dossier had not retrieved.

sources.title: 1ST MPUMALANGA GAY PRIDE A SUCCESS (MambaOnline)
sources.summary: MambaOnline (11 September 2014) reports that Mpumalanga's first LGBTI Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital Nelspruit (Mbombela) under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United', with around 1,000 participants marching from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza and a post-parade picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. Organiser Joy Kunene said police were 'visible and supportive' and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers to assist, and the march launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations. The event is direct evidence of a public, police-supported LGBTIQ+ presence in the province's capital, tempering the record's picture of exclusively hostile local institutions.

sources.title: LGBTIQ+ community speak about discrimination at police in eMbalenhle (Ridge Times)
sources.summary: Ridge Times (29 August 2026) reports that at the Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations; participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after being sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. The report, from the Secunda-area local press, documents current, province-specific LGBTIQ+ grievances about police treatment in Mpumalanga — the kind of enforcement-facing finding this record lacked.

76434192B37104984973577.name: Limpopo
76434192B37104984973577.summary:
For a trans traveller in the rural parts of this province, the practical risk is the parallel customary-authority system rather than ordinary criminal law: no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded, but chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. An analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system' for people in the former Bantustans and threatens to undermine security 'for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights'. For an outed visitor in a rural area, the moral authority a complaint lands before is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court, and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual.

The legal baseline behind that system is in flux: the legislation was enacted in 2019 and declared unconstitutional in 2023 by the national court, with the declaration suspended while a replacement is prepared - reducing but not eliminating the parallel-system concern a visitor faces in rural areas. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.

sources.summary: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

Mamba Online (18 Apr 2012, Melanie Judge): the Traditional Courts Bill debated in provincial public hearings would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system; lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out, so those who can are expected to leave rural areas; traditional leaders also opposed the 2006 Civil Union Act. Direct support for the record's rural-traditional-courts risk assessment.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
North West sits squarely in the former-Bantustan geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the Bantustan-era map: HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in South Africa. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

North West is also the only province outside Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010; the GALA-hosted Love Not Hate review records only three quantitative studies ever attempted nationally), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the "dark figure" of unreported crime that characterises most provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65), the two share the former-Bantustan customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; North West's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above Limpopo because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), North West sits higher because KZN adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA official alignment against queer people; North West has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. vs. Western Cape (0.72) and Gauteng (0.71), the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat applies equally: a province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting than more danger.

sources.title: North West trans community desperate for hormone replacement services
sources.summary: The trans community in North West province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to get it, MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the SA Human Rights Commission. Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

sources.title: Lesbian pupil banned from school in North West
sources.summary: MambaOnline (23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News) reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village, North West, was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl', and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a North West institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

sources.title: New Report on LGBT Community in North West
sources.summary: A report entitled 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010, presented the results of a survey conducted under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology during 2009 and 2010, with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella collaborating; it surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination. Provides the province-level 2010 survey behind this record's data-presence signal for North West.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.

sources.summary: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

sources.title: Transgender Woman in Brutal Hate Crime Attack in Tshwane Tavern
sources.summary: Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane, Gauteng), was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline (6 January 2025) reported had shown no progress. The province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities
sources.summary: The SA Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism (14 November 2025) welcomed the judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), delivered on 10 November 2025. The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. Demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and national 7). The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk; Paris alone records 22 per 100,000 but the official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). Île-de-France has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere in metropolitan France.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The dossier's own caveat is explicit: "high recorded rates in Paris should not be read as Paris being dangerous." Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the state actively banned assembly; Île-de-France's state response to Pride was protective if tense. Compare with PACA (0.65), which shares the metro-rate exposure but adds the Fréjus dress-code incident as a specific negative on public appearance.

sources.summary: Interior-ministry statistics service (SSMSI) Infraction rapide n°53, May 2025: 4,800 recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in France in 2024 (+5% on 2023; crimes/délicts up 14%/year since 2016); only about 4% of victims file complaints; acts concentrate in urban units over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris — whose rate, 22 per 100,000 against the national 7, the note attributes partly to non-resident victims and commuters; recorded victims are >70% men.

franceinfo (June 2025): Paris Pride (Marche des fierte, 28 June 2025) was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry; CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march, with police framed as separating opposing groups and extremists as the enemy. Visitor-relevant: big LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response.

sources.title: LGBTQ culture in Paris - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia (LGBTQ culture in Paris): Paris concentrates France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure - as of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, it hosts France's only officially organised gaybourhoods, and it stages the annual Paris Pride parade (La Marche des Fiertés). The article also records that Bertrand Delanoë became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002 and was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals - dated evidence that even the country's most LGBTQ-visible city carries a targeted-violence history a visitor should weigh.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in France - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia (LGBTQ rights in France), the national framework a traveller in Île-de-France stands under: France introduced same-sex civil partnerships (PACS) in 1999 and became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage in 2013, with anti-discrimination protections on grounds of sexual orientation (1985) and gender identity (2012). Since 2017 transgender people may change their legal gender without surgery or any medical diagnosis, and in 2010 France was the first country in the world to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness. This supplies the legal baseline behind the record's national score (0.67) for travel-with-partner and documentation purposes.

28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017): documents the Feb 2017 Chechen police purge — men believed gay rounded up, held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured; some forcibly disappeared, others returned to families 'barely alive from beatings', captors outing them and urging honour killings. Report shows Kadyrov's denial notwithstanding that top regional officials knew. The core sourced basis for this record's extreme-risk profile.

Novaya Gazeta (11 Jan 2019, Russian): learned of renewed persecution of gay men in Chechnya — warnings circulated via VKontakte LGBT-group admins telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. Follows the paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men for which no criminal case was opened. Establishes the purge reactivated within two years, not a one-off.

The Insider (4 Sep 2024): SK SOS reports Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service — at least seven sent to frontlines in Ukraine, one already killed; methods began before the 21 Sep 2022 mobilisation order. In early Sep 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they'd be sent to front. Establishes detention-to-frontline blackmail as an ongoing persecution vector since 2022.

OC Media (Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation): a mass wave of unlawful detentions sweeping Chechnya with detainees forcibly sent to fight in Ukraine — people detained over minor pretexts (missing insurance documents), taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, forced to sign contracts; families sometimes must recruit two 'volunteers' to free a detained relative. Complements the gay-specific coercion reports: conscription machinery as a generalised coercive tool of the Chechen security apparatus.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; notes the 2023 'extremist organisation' designation of the international LGBT+ movement exposing support/activity to 2–6 years (organising 6–10) imprisonment, with violence spreading beyond the region. The freshest official-assessment source for the record's trans-specific claim.

Stavropol Krai is named in the Canadian travel advisory's special-permission requirement (alongside Chechnya, Dagestan, and Ingushetia) and is included in the North Caucasus zone identified by the UK Home Office CPIN as the exception to Russia's general risk picture. The dossier specifically identifies the south-eastern part bordering Chechnya as subject to the same security-and-custom enforcement logic. However, Stavropol is a krai, not a republic, and the extreme documented violence (secret prisons, purges, coerced conscription) is Chechen-specific rather than krai-wide.

For a visitor, the special-permission regime itself restricts movement and independent oversight, and the south-eastern areas adjacent to Chechnya share the localised security culture. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.05 below. Above the core North Caucasus republics (Dagestan, Ingushetia at 0.04; Kabardino-Balkaria, Karachay-Cherkessia, North Ossetia at 0.05) because the extreme evidence is geographically limited to the Chechnya border zone within a large multi-ethnic krai, and no independent republic-level security apparatus analogous to Kadyrov's exists.

sources.summary: Global Affairs Canada Russia advisory (retrieved): avoid-all-travel; frequent terrorist attacks named for Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and the Stavropol region; MOI special permission required to enter certain areas (list: Kabardino-Balkaria incl. Elbrus, Karachai-Cherkessia, North Ossetia); 2SLGBTQI+ persons/ally families attacked, harassed and abused; since Jan 2024 advocacy organisations treated as 'extremist'; foreigner surveillance warned.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): singles out the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates there likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation → 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment.

Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; year-on-year deterioration from an on-the-ground defender in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's Russia country overview records the federal framework a Moscow visitor stands under: the Supreme Court in November 2023 declared the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and on 22 March 2024 it was formally added to the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations, a designation the page says has led to arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols on extremism charges. 28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in Russia (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a Siberian court in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
For a trans visitor, the capital region offers the strongest local protections in the country, but they are city-scoped: in July 2025 a city of the region became the first local government unit to enact a gender-inclusive health ordinance, creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care, mental-health support and specialist services through the city's public-health system - the only enforceable institutional recourse a discovered visitor can find in the country, invoked through the city's complaint machinery. The national picture otherwise is violence against trans women, documented in a 2024-2025 series of killings without dependable local machinery; the memorial record lists a 29-year-old trans woman strangled during a drinking session in a capital-region city on 1 March 2024.

Protection is real but partial for a traveller: a functioning framework on paper in the country's largest city, with an enforcement-and-services reality that does not yet extend past city limits; no national anti-discrimination statute covers gender identity, and no visitor documents or border-screening practice is recorded for the region.

Transrespectful/trans murder documentation site (TDoR2 memorial) report entry: Shaina Bayabay, 29, Pasig City, Metro Manila, Philippines - 1 March 2024, category violence, cause strangled; the underlying report adds that she was killed during a drinking session.

36201628B88329767373181.name: Central Visayas
36201628B88329767373181.summary:
Central Visayas holds the most active provincial-level anti-discrimination ordinance cluster outside the capital region: Mandaue City signed the Implementation Rules and Regulations of the Anti-Discrimination Ordinance in July 2024, formalised jointly with the city mayor, the KAABAG LGBT Federation and a UN development programme — an operational, not merely symbolic, local protection in the Cebu metro. The municipality of Carmen, northern Cebu, approved a Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Ordinance protecting people on SOGIE grounds by unanimous Sangguniang Bayan vote in June 2025, days before the end of Pride month. A visitor in Cebu or Mandaue can invoke an operational anti-discrimination ordinance.

No killings, assaults or institutional-hostility incidents specific to trans visitors or residents are documented in this region within the 2024-2025 national violence series or elsewhere in the research record — protection without any accompanying regional violence signal.

36201628B76469343449086.name: Soccsksargen
36201628B76469343449086.summary:
In June 2025 a transgender-rights activist was shot dead in General Santos City. Human Rights Watch, an international human-rights organisation, called the killing an "apparent targeted killing" and said police were examining her activism as a possible motive; the national Commission on Human Rights publicly condemned the killings of two transgender women as "marked by cruelty and impunity" and named her. The killing stood unresolved as of the record's sources, and no protective ordinance or institutional counterweight is documented in this region.

For a trans visitor the finding is targeted lethal violence against activists in a province with an official acknowledgement of impunity and no local machinery to answer it.

sources.title: Municipal Ordinance No. 15, Series of 2023, Municipality of Bayambang, Pangasinan — An Ordinance Protecting the Rights of Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, Transgenders, Queers and Intersex (LGBTQI) in the Municipality of Bayambang Against Any and All Forms of Discrimination Solely on the Basis of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, Expression, Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC) and Providing Penalties for Violation Thereof (certified copy)
sources.summary: The certified eight-page copy of Bayambang Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, protects LGBTQI persons in the municipality against discrimination 'solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression, sex characteristics (SOGIESC)' and sets a penalty ladder: first offence a fine of at least Php1,000 or one month's imprisonment; second offence at least Php2,000 or one month-and-a-day to six months; third offence at least Php2,500 or six months-and-a-day to eight months; later violations one year's imprisonment plus at least Php2,500; violators must also complete mandatory human rights education. Complaints are filed through the barangay (Katarungang Pambarangay) mechanism under R.A. 7160, giving a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor an actual local complaint route. 68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.

For the record: the sharpest local hostility in South Korea — state-adjacent opposition recurring annually but judicially contained each time.

Kidok (Korean Christian daily, September 2025): a Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer' response to the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans.

The page records that such opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street, and it carries survey context on national attitudes (Pew Research Center: 18% of South Koreans felt homosexuality should be tolerated in 2007, rising to 39% in 2013). sources.summary: No Cut News (English, 8 June 2026): the Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters — comprising the Daegu–Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association — filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea (NHRCK) demanding a change of venue for the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, claiming the event is likely to infringe on public welfare; the group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single NHRCK petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Daegu's Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It counteracts the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act. Dated court-and-petition evidence that official venue restriction and organised anti-queer mobilisation over the festival continued into the 2026 edition, directly supporting this record's account of a confrontational environment around the event.

For a trans visitor, this province's standing is origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors: the model student human-rights ordinance — covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity — was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for this province, and the province stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances when the capital abolished its own in April 2024.

The protections credited to the province bear on enrolled students and school staff, not on visitors; no visitor-facing enforcement action, arrest, or incident is documented for this unit, and a teacher based in the province warned that wholesale abolition of such ordinances 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. No visitor documents, border-screening practice, or marriage/partner-travel provision is recorded in the dossier.

sources.summary: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.

Separately, Concepción's municipality dismissed the staff of its Oficina de la Diversidad y No Discriminación during the January 2025 honourary-staff cuts (~100 workers), which LGBTIQA+ organisations called a "dismantling" leaving one person in post.

Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), Bío-Bío is 0.06 higher: Valparaíso's problem is the volume of over half the national case load, while Bío-Bío has specific institutional incidents but a normalised share. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Bío-Bío is 0.02 lower: Tarapacá's finding is a judicial annulment that devalues trans life in theory, whereas Bío-Bío's hospital episode shows how that devaluation manifests in the care a visitor might actually receive.

Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: only 157 people used the Gender Identity Law (21.120) for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), La Araucanía is 0.01 higher: Tarapacá carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas Araucanía's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because Araucanía's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

For a visitor, the practical implication is not a specific hostile incident but the trajectory: the fastest-rising region with the thinnest LGBTI support infrastructure and least public visibility means fewer allies, fewer complaint channels, and a deteriorating climate without institutional counterweight.

10402087B60477050509260.name: Bayern
10402087B60477050509260.summary:
Since 1 April 2024, gender-inclusive German is prohibited in schools, universities and all state administration: the ban implements a December 2023 government declaration through a cabinet decision amending the language rules of public authorities, and its practical reach extends across every public counter, registry office and classroom a visitor might deal with, even though critics dismiss the measure as symbol politics.

The legal baseline a visitor stands under is the national Self-Determination Act, in force since 1 November 2024: adults over 18 may change first name and legal gender by self-declaration with three months' notice, same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and in goods and services. For a trans visitor the operative regional signal is therefore administrative-interface restriction on gender-inclusive language rather than any change to the national legal floor.

Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods/services, though the page notes some protections vary by region. sources.title: Selbstbestimmungsgesetz

It passed the Bundestag on 12 April 2024 (374-251, 11 abstentions) and the Bundesrat on 17 May 2024, was gazetted 21 June 2024; changes could be registered from 1 August 2024 and took effect 1 November 2024. Adults declare the change themselves before the registry office; 14-17 year-olds need a guardian's (or the family court's) consent; for under-14s only the guardian can declare, and a three-month waiting period applies with a one-year lockout after a change. The article also records the Bundesrat's 20 October 2023 criticism that the draft let parents decide under-14 gender-entry changes 'without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare' - exactly the contested point behind the Bavarian-led tightening initiative this record covers.

10402087B20892132820961.name: Berlin
10402087B20892132820961.summary:
Germany's Pride movement faces a documented rise in attacks: the amadeu-antonio-stiftung counted 55 right-wing-motivated attacks on Pride events nationally in 2024 and 30 in 2025 across roughly 120 parades, including a boiling-water attack, and runs a €100,000 support fund weighted to eastern Germany. Ahead of the 2025 Christopher Street Day, with hundreds of thousands expected, Berlin's organisers nonetheless urged participants to 'be vigilant'.

The reporting also situates the capital: Maneo, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades like Berlin's had not been specifically threatened — smaller towns are hardest to police — while everyday hostility still surfaces: one Berlin-Neukölln queer café owner reports 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in eighteen months.

MANEO says the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and that the counselling centre itself was attacked several times in 2025. This is the primary Berlin project behind the record's claim that documented homophobic violence in the capital is rising, and it names Neukölln - the record's café-owner example - among the worst-hit districts.

10402087B40185768535592.summary:
In Cottbus on 20 October 2025, a rubbish container was set alight against the façade of the 'Regenbogenkombinat' queer cultural centre during CSD week; the fire was out in about fifteen minutes and nobody was hurt, but state security (Staatsschutz) took over the arson investigation and a political motive cannot be excluded — local initiatives call it an attempted firebombing, and the attack sits among earlier suspected far-right attacks in the city.

The local queer community describes itself as unusually watchful: repeated physical pressure on infrastructure, met by a functioning protective response.

10402087B85226028911536.name: Hessen
10402087B85226028911536.summary:
A Hessen Landtag small inquiry with the Interior Minister's answer (April 2025) records police-registered queer-hostile offences rising from 33 in 2022 to 83 in 2023 and 135 in 2024 — a year-on-year jump of 52 that the minister's reply calls alarming.

The trend must be read with the federal BKA's own caveat: its situation report on LSBTIQ* security introduced a new reporting category that makes state-by-state comparison possible but warns that classification changes can inflate registered counts, so rises may partly reflect better recording rather than a sharper danger. The same answer notes the 2010-established network of LSBTIQ* liaison officers in every police headquarters, governed by a standing framework concept — an institutional response in place while the statistics remain ambiguous.

Interior Minister Roman Poseck (CDU) called the development 'alarmierend', attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces, and the ministry counted suspects identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings and six convictions. This is the media confirmation of the record's police-registered 33 (2022) to 83 (2023) to 135 (2024) series.

The article notes Hessen police keep dedicated contact officers for this hate crime and the state government promises consistent prosecution. It updates the record's statistics with the 2025 figure of 141 and confirms the state's own alarm at the trend.

10402087B67217417145666.name: Thüringen
10402087B67217417145666.summary:
The regional parliament of Thüringen exhibits formal, multi-layered hostility to gender policy: a far-right faction motion demands consistent implementation of a ban on gender-inclusive language in Thuringian schools, asserting schools must not be 'a socio-political experimental field', and a draft law proposes to dismantle the region's existing equality-policy machinery, arguing that current law 'regularly violates the principle of equal opportunity'. The dossier characterises this parliament as formally hostile to gender policy.

The draft law is the most consequential institutional signal in this dossier for a visitor: if enacted, a trans person reporting an incident would find no regional equality apparatus to complain to, and the gender-language motion compounds that at the administrative and reporting interface. 14339913B89763821047858.name: Wales
14339913B89763821047858.summary:
Wales's devolved administration has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the parent nation's post-judgment years: the plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, and a dedicated young-people's edition was posted in January 2026.

The statutory school guidance 'Rights, Respect, Equality' (consultation May 2025) obliges schools to challenge bullying and harassment on the grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, with incident recording and monitoring and a parental escalation route. The practical facility rules are unchanged here, so the official posture is inclusion at a national moment of rollback, and for a visitor that registers only as a protective institutional climate.

The legal floor a visitor stands under includes civil partnerships (since 2005) and same-sex marriage (since 2014), the legal right to change gender (since 2004), an equalised age of consent (since 2001) and discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity; a first gender-identity clinic opened locally in September 2019.

The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). It records the surrounding UK rollback — the UK Government blocking the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023 — while Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, with parents of transgender children calling for more help (BBC, March 2024). 14339913B6930312138089.name: Northern Ireland
14339913B6930312138089.summary:
Northern Ireland carries three sub-national negatives absent elsewhere in the UK: Education Minister Paul Givan ordered the 2019 transgender-pupils guidance withdrawn from the Education Authority website in September 2025 after the FWS ruling, calling it "unlawful and flawed" and a product of "activist campaigns"; the Justice Minister's attempt to include transgender people as a protected group in hate-crime sentencing reform was stalled (reported DUP obstruction); and the Rainbow Project records a pattern of paramilitary-flavoured anti-LGB&T violence including a pipe bomb thrown through the home of a trans woman in Derry/Londonderry described by PSNI as a "sectarian hate crime," a 2019 Belfast city-centre assault hospitalising a gay man, and an average of ~290 anti-LGB&T incidents per year (2013–2017) with rising transgender-identity strand counts to September 2025.

Counter-balancing: PSNI/NISRA track a separate "transgender identity" category (unlike England and Wales), evidencing institutional recognition; the Health Minister publicly defended gender-identity service funding (£800k+ uplift) against DUP/TUV criticism, showing the executive is split rather than uniformly hostile. No criminal ban on expression or police-enforced facility prohibition exists — the risk mechanism mirrors the national EHRC code (service refusal by staff) plus street-level violence.

BBC News (14 December 2025): other executive parties blocked justice minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation (approval sought early November, response deadline mid-November; bill had executive agreement from December 2024). Long cited PSNI statistics of close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 in force 27 July 2026) removed the civil provision making it unlawful to "offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate" a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, including gender identity. The NT is the only Australian jurisdiction that has actively reversed anti-discrimination protection rather than extended it; the government framed the rollback as "restoring freedom of speech and religion." For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is now deliberately outside NT law while other states have brought it inside.

Federal protections continue to apply uniformly: the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 covers gender identity in every state and territory, and NT hate-crime penalty enhancements for SO/GI-motivated offences (2022 amendment, effective 2023) remain in force. No criminal expression ban, no facility-access ban, and no conversion-practice-specific enforcement issue arises for a short-term visitor beyond the general federal framework.

Remote-area context amplifies practical risk: Alice Springs records approximately 2,600+ offences against a population of ~25,000, and trans community infrastructure in the NT is thin. A single domestic killing of a Tiwi Sistergirl (Darwin, October 2024) is recorded for completeness but is one non-patterned incident and does not support a regional violence finding on its own.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the NT sits 0.09 below: the deliberate legislative removal of the "offend, insult, humiliate" protection is the strongest negative sub-national signal in Australia, even though it is a civil-law rollback rather than a criminal prohibition. Vs Victoria (0.88), where the 2025 Anti-Vilification Act created the country's first criminal offence for public incitement against a trans person, the NT moved in the opposite direction in the same year.

ABC News, 17 Oct 2025: the NT government's anti-discrimination amendments passed parliament, framed as restoring free speech and religious freedom — narrowing the vilification provision and letting religious schools prefer staff sharing the same faith; the government had earlier backtracked from scrapping the vilification section. sources.summary: The jurisdiction status page documents the NT timeline behind this record's assessment: male homosexual activity legal since 1 January 1984 with an equal age of consent since 2003; same-sex marriage from nationwide December 2017 (the territory's postal-survey 'Yes' was 60.6%); full adoption rights since 2018; birth-certificate sex-marker change requiring clinical treatment since 2018; and territory discrimination protections since 2022, with a March 2025 government announcement and July 2025 bill to repeal the vilification ('offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate') provision. It also records that the NT government banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals in February 2025, issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors, and that the territory's own hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity (federal coverage of those motives only since 2025). The page independently corroborates the record's central claim that the NT is actively reversing, not extending, anti-discrimination protection.

sources.title: NT's CLP government confirms plans to scrap Labor's hate speech changes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News, 2 March 2025: the Country Liberal Party government confirmed it would repeal the vilification provision Labor added to NT anti-discrimination law three years earlier, which made it unlawful to 'offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate' a person because of a characteristic such as race or gender and could trigger action by the NT Anti-Discrimination Commission; Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby framed the change as restoring 'freedom of speech and religion', including letting religious schools again hire only co-religionists. NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the move, warning the government may be 'opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech'. This is the March 2025 announcement that set in motion the rollback this record describes, which the Wikipedia/legislation trail confirms was enacted as the Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (assented 30 October 2025).

82085004B60194602145168.name: Victoria
82085004B60194602145168.summary:
Victoria's Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025, created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, plus personal association; the civil grounds commenced 15 April 2026. The state human-rights commission's explainer records public incitement against a trans person becoming criminally chargeable alongside civil recourse.

Practical safety context: a coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women during the pandemic found the state police failed the search for one of them (missing December 2020), and the coroner made nine recommendations including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons risk practice; the state government is reviewing them. The inquest documents a serious institutional failure, and the 2025 legislation and the review process are the corrective response. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this state is recorded in the dossier.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024, in force since 4 April 2025, makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person out of the state for the purpose or engaging a provider outside the state for it (taking a person out of the state for the purpose carries up to three years); a civil complaints scheme runs through the state anti-discrimination body. The state also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Violence context: a trans woman was killed in her apartment in January 2020, and the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and went to a murder trial — a positive institutional response. In a second case a trans woman who had arrived in the country roughly six weeks earlier was strangled, and her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that media reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in this state within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents.

No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this state is recorded in the dossier; the operative visitor-facing exposure is the violence pattern and the criminal conversion-practices ban rather than any state-specific document or travel rule.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Western Australia's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute of 'gender history', defined by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex — a narrower, medically-inflected, binary formulation than the 'gender identity' language used in other Australian jurisdictions and in the federal Sex Discrimination Act. A non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may not meet the state-law definition and would rely solely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint; there is no state anti-vilification offence (civil or criminal) and no statutory charter binding public authorities.

Reform is underway: a registration amendment act received assent on 26 September 2024, removing medical and surgical prerequisites for registration of a sex or gender change, with substantive commencement still by proclamation; it is not yet fully in force as of the scoring date, so the narrower 'gender history' definition remains the operative complaints route a visitor stands under.

Complaints mechanics: a state complaint runs to the state equal-opportunity commission under the Equal Opportunity Act with a 12-month lodgement window, a one-week acknowledgement and a free conciliation conference; the alternative federal route runs to the national human-rights commission under the Sex Discrimination Act within 24 months (12 months for employment), and only one route may be chosen.

WA Government guidance (first published 6 Aug 2020, last updated 12 Feb 2026): gender history is a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) — a person has gender history if they identify as a member of the opposite sex by living or seeking to live as such; direct discrimination (including treating a person as their former sex) and indirect discrimination are unlawful.

sources.title: Reforms to remove barriers for LGBTQIA+ community | Western Australian Government
sources.summary: WA Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced on 16 April 2024 that the Births, Deaths, Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024 would be introduced to State Parliament that week, repealing the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishing the Gender Reassignment Board - which they say makes WA the only remaining Australian jurisdiction with such a board - in favour of a streamlined administrative process via the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Applicants would no longer need medical or surgical reassignment, providing instead a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling; a 'non-binary' sex descriptor would become available, stricter rules apply to under-18s (parental consent or Family Court of WA permission), and the Bill contains a statutory review clause after three years. The announcement implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations and links the reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a conversion-practices ban in 2025. This is the official government source for the record's claim that the 2024 Act removes medical and surgical prerequisites for registering a sex or gender change in Western Australia.

sources.title: Equal Opportunity Commission Fact Sheet - Gender Reassigned Person Discrimination | Western Australian Government
sources.summary: The WA Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet states that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (WA), recently passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, amends the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) at section 4(1) by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a new definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. It warns the amendment will not operate retrospectively and that 'gender history' discrimination complaints under the Equal Opportunity Act will need to be made in compliance with the new registration requirements once the Act commences, and notes the Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001. This primary government document confirms the record's claim that the 2024 reform feeds back into the scope of WA's 'gender history' attribute for complaints purposes and that substantive commencement is by proclamation.

The resource names trans-specific local support in WA (TransFolk of WA, the Freedom Centre for under-26s). This confirms the record's claim that 'gender history' rather than 'gender identity' is the state-level protective attribute in WA and that state complaints run through the Equal Opportunity Commission.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
The territory's Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, giving a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or public facility a legal review mechanism that common-law states without a charter lack. The territory is also one of four jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for this territory; the absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and the self-identification custody rule, places it modestly above the national average.

A conversion-practices ban has been in force since early 2021, with offending practices attracting up to a 12-month custodial term or a fine, alongside civil penalties giving a tribunal power to issue orders and order redress; practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this territory is recorded in the dossier.

This is the primary legal source for the record's claim that the ACT has its own Human Rights Act 2004 as the statutory rights framework public authorities must operate within.

sources.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. This is the first documented ACT-specific institutional-capacity finding and qualifies the record's claim that no countervailing region-specific finding was identified for the ACT.

sources.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. This dated ACT criminal statute supports the record's characterisation of the ACT as a protective rights jurisdiction and adds to the territory's structural positives beyond the Human Rights Act and self-identification custody rule.

25490228B8471183517505.name: Castilla y León
25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community that has never enacted a regional LGTBI or gender-identity law, and for a transgender visitor that vacuum has a practical administrative meaning: no dedicated regional equality office exists to receive a complaint, there is no institutional hate-crime observatory, and no region-specific administrative protocol governs responses to gender-motivated incidents. No criminal ban or facility restriction exists in the region, national criminal law fully applies, and the severity floor is therefore set by the state; the recorded deviation of approximately −0.07 from the national score (0.88) reflects sub-national administrative coldness and rural exposure rather than any region-specific criminal threat.

The pending regional LGTBI+ equality bill (registered December 2024, in processing since 11 June 2025) is framed around ending the sexilio — the documented exodus of LGBT people, especially the young, from the region's rural areas to larger cities — a resident-facing concern rather than a visitor protection; until it is enacted, a transgender traveller facing discrimination has no dedicated regional channel beyond the national institutions, and the protective infrastructure is thinnest in the rural areas where the exodus pattern is documented.

sources.summary: Europa Press (Valladolid, 11 Jun 2025): the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the PSOE-sponsored LGTBI+ bill into consideration (76 articles) after the PP abstained; the bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands.

Salamancahoy (20 Dec 2024): the PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for real and effective equality of LGTBI+ people in Castilla y León, aiming to end the "sexilio" (out-migration of LGBTI people from the region), one of three bills tabled that week; group leader Tudanca urged fastest possible processing.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 Jun 2025): the plenary approved taking the LGTBI equality bill into debate with opposition support except Vox and PP abstention; LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee. Same vote as the Europa Press report, adding civil-society reaction.

25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Ceuta, an autonomous city rather than a comunidad autónoma, has no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute — a framework gap it shares with its neighbouring city Melilla and with Castilla y León, recorded in the national regional-law inventories as a gap case only. No incident evidence, no enforcement data and no hate-offence figure separating the city from the national aggregate was retrievable, so this is a statute-book gap, explicitly not an incident finding. National criminal law and the national police still operate here, so the enforcement floor for a transgender visitor is unchanged from the rest of the country; unlike some communities, the city has no regional equality office, LGTBI observatory or police force of its own.

The border-fence crossing environment and the city's religious-minority composition create a document-and-presentation context different from the rest of the country, adding modest friction for a visitor whose identity documents do not match presentation. The one LGTBI-specific episode the dossier records for the city concerns migrants remaining there after an irregular-entry wave, not visitor incidents.

sources.summary: The national-framework page (in-scope for Melilla because it states the law a visitor there stands under) records that a registry for unmarried same-sex couples was created in the autonomous city of Melilla in 2008 — alongside Ceuta (1998) and all 17 mainland communities — granting unmarried couples benefits the page calls mainly symbolic; that is the only Melilla-specific legal datapoint the page carries, and it is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute, consistent with this record's legislative-silence finding. The page also documents the framework that applies uniformly in Melilla: same-sex marriage and adoption nationwide since July 2005; hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity banned since 1995 with crime-law penalty enhancements for such motives; and legal-gender self-determination on documents without surgery or sterilisation since the trans law approved 16 February 2023 (vote 191-60 with 91 abstentions, applying to people over 16). For this record it substantiates the claim that national criminal and equality law and the state police still govern in Melilla, while confirming no regional trans or LGTBI statute exists there.
