15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
In August 2026 the Kelantan assembly passed a new Syariah Criminal Offences Bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state's syariah jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state's 2019 syariah criminal code that Malaysia's Federal Court had struck down as outside state power. The Bill also carries "protection of modesty" decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years.

The sequence — invalidation by the federal courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to syariah proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.

sources.summary: Kelantan's newly passed Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 (passed Aug 2026) contains provisions on covering aurat (modesty), gender change, and safeguarding the modesty of private parts, replacing 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 struck down by the Federal Court. Clause 15 mandates Muslims safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law. For this record: the state's legislative direction explicitly regulates gender-change matters under Islamic criminal law, with enforcement beginning 2026.

Follow-up report confirms Kelantan passed strict new decency rules via the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 (13 Aug 2026), legislating decency, aurat-covering, and gender-change provisions; the enactment replaces 16 provisions of the 2019 enactment struck down by the Federal Court. The article also notes a related Feb 2026 first Kelantan Syariah Court case involving gender change. For this record: confirms the new decency/gender-change legislation is now in force and being applied by the Syariah courts.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
In May 2025 the city authority of the state capital erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a 'constant reminder' to steer people away from homosexuality. A transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.

The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences the state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary religious-law offences and the national criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What a transgender visitor meets here is open, ongoing official hostility, including state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.

sources.summary: A Terengganu state executive councillor (May 2025) openly confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices installed at strategic locations in the state are intended to instil hatred of homosexual acts, saying the state wants people to consider the acts 'dirty, wrong, and to be avoided'. For this record: official state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging — a direct indicator of the hostile official stance a transgender visitor faces in Terengganu.

Thirteen civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters (May 2025) urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove anti-LGBT signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law; they criticised the Terengganu state executive councillor's defence of the signboards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. For this record: corroborates the official anti-LGBT campaign in Terengganu and documents civil-society pushback with named actors.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for 'encouraging vice'. The raid's design — isolating transgender women as a category from a mixed party — evidences enforcement capacity and willingness aimed at transgender people specifically. A coalition of national human-rights organisations publicly protested, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves.

The legal baseline for a visitor: the state's 2014 religious criminal enactment criminalises same-sex conduct (liable to fines, imprisonment or whipping) and criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, while female cross-dressing is not criminalised; a transgender visitor whose public presentation does not match her assigned sex is directly exposed under that provision, and same-sex conduct offences apply to a visiting couple as they do to residents.

sources.summary: The page's dedicated Kedah section reports the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014): liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex) are criminalised under sections 23 and 24, punishable by up to RM5,000 fine, up to 3 years' imprisonment, or up to 6 strokes of whipping (or any combination); a male posing as a woman in public is criminalised under section 26 (up to RM1,000 fine or up to 1 year imprisonment), while female cross-dressing is not; women convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to 6 months under section 52. For this record: Kedah-specific state criminal law covering same-sex conduct and trans male-to-female public presentation, the direct legal risk a trans visitor faces in this state.

65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by Pelangi Nusantara — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ('Bogor clean of LGBT'). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law — Amnesty demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to Perpres 111/2025, which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: 'people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence.' The pattern-plus-impunity combination is West Java-specific; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.

A trans woman quoted says those who previously appeared in public now live in fear. For this record: documents street violence against trans women within the region and the national regulatory backdrop enabling it.

Tempo (25-26 June 2025): Indonesian police detained 75 people at a villa in Puncak, Bogor Regency, West Java, at a gathering police called an LGBT 'family gathering' held 'to avoid detection'; West Java Regional Police confirmed the June 22, 2025 arrests, which followed a tip from local residents. For this record: a concrete 2025 enforcement action against an LGBT gathering inside the region, showing police actively investigate and detain LGBT gatherings in West Java.

Amnesty International (24 June 2025) condemned the arrest of 75 people in the raid on a privately rented villa in Puncak, Bogor, West Java, calling it a discriminatory raid and 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' exemplifying the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia; Amnesty said the gathering violated no law and demanded release and accountability. For this record: international framing of the West Java raid as unlawful, reinforcing that LGBTI gatherings in the region face police action despite violating no law.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. Enforcement is real but contested: a 2026 field study of the Perda's implementation reports supervision, enforcement and guidance by the local order force (Satpol PP), with sanctions of suboptimal effectiveness and rehabilitation hampered because the facilities barely exist; a 2025 study records people recorded as swept up in LGBT sweeps/app findings jumping from 56 in 2023 to 272 in 2024, and customary-law actors pushing parallel measures (a boarding-house barcode system, proposed nagari regulations on social deviance). Limapuluh Kota regency finalised a draft (ranperda, articles 13-14) on public tranquility containing an explicit LGBT prohibition with administrative fines in the tens of millions of rupiah plus mandated "rehabilitation" (psychosocial counselling, spiritual guidance, resocialisation) for people of same-sex attraction. OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation mapping of discriminatory regional regulations covers eight other provinces (not West Sumatra itself, whose key bylaws postdate the study), but documents the same regional-autonomy mechanism this province's bylaws instantiate.

This sits below the national score because an enacted bylaw with specified sanctions creates visitor-facing risk (detention, forced rehabilitation programmes, fines) that does not exist in most provinces; the documented apprehension counts show the bylaw environment is actively policed, though no caning (an Aceh-specific penalty) or prosecution under these provisions is recorded. It remains above West Java (0.06), where patterned mob violence with zero accountability is the primary threat, and above the national floor where no such bylaw exists at all.

sources.summary: Academic article (AHKAM journal) analysing Bukittinggi City (West Sumatra) Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order targeting LGBT, examined from the perspective of Fiqih Siyasah Tanfidziyah (implementation of Islamic governance): the regulation is framed as responding to local religious values and Minangkabau customs. For this record: documents a 2024 local anti-LGBT public-order regulation in a West Sumatra city, showing formal municipal-level restrictions.

Peer-reviewed study (2025) of LGBT cases in Bukittinggi City, West Sumatra: recorded cases rose from 56 individuals in 2023 to 272 in 2024; the Kurai Customary Law Community (Masyarakat Hukum Adat Kurai) acts as a non-state actor, initiating the customary sanction 'dibuang sepanjang adat' (expulsion under adat), proposing village regulations on social deviance, and implementing barcode monitoring in boarding houses to police LGBT presence. For this record: documents rising state-and-adat surveillance and customary sanctions against LGBT people within a West Sumatra city.

Mimbarsumbar.id (13 May 2026): the DPRD (regional legislature) of Limapuluh Kota regency, West Sumatra, finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation (Ranperda) within a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, including administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people; the drafting body chair stated stages have reached finalisation. For this record: a 2026 draft provincial-level regulation introducing fines and 'rehabilitation' targeting LGBT people in a West Sumatra regency.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra, Yogyakarta) - the reference for Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism; West Sumatra's newer Bukittinggi regulation postdates the mapping.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.

sources.summary: Peer-reviewed article (Anthropology of the Middle East, 2025) on the 'precarious lives' of the transpuan (trans feminine) community in Indonesia based on four ethnographic case studies in Bali: documents how transpuan people navigate circumstances marked by both resistance and misrecognition and discrimination, challenging the narrative of victimhood while showing real precarity. For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

Travel guide (Gayborhood/Traven) on Bali: ranks the destination '6.3/10' with a legal score of 2.0, warning same-sex relations are criminalised in Indonesia and that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risks; advises visitors to 'keep your love a little quieter' despite the island's tolerant reputation. For this record: practical traveller-facing warning that Bali's legal backdrop (Indonesian national law) carries criminalisation risk even where the local scene is accepting.

Travel guide (Mar 2026): Bali is broadly welcoming to LGBTQ+ travellers on a 'live and let live' basis, and same-sex relationships are not a criminal offence in Bali under Indonesian national law, though the new Criminal Code (KUHP, in effect Jan 2026) adds complexity; same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia; Seminyak (Eat Street/Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, while public displays of affection warrant discretion. For this record: current, specific traveller guidance for trans/LGBTQ visitors to Bali including the 2026 KUHP law change.

65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.

Human Rights Monitor Papua Quarterly Report Q3 2025 (31 Oct 2025) on West Papua: documents killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and the failure of accountability mechanisms by security forces expanding across the territory, plus a healthcare crisis under scrutiny and arrests of protesters. Contains no trans/LGBTI-specific findings. For this record: indicates a high-violence, low-accountability security climate in West Papua relevant to overall traveller safety, but provides no trans-specific substance.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), and the page names Papua among the provinces whose trans residents have benefited (with Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung); only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained. The same page's national-framework facts apply in Papua: the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage (up to one year in prison) takes effect on 2 January 2026, same-sex marriage is not recognised, and customary laws may apply. For this record: evidence that trans people in Papua may obtain identity documents through the national outreach programme, and the national legal framework a trans visitor stands under while in the province.

65028918B17554737605304.name: South Sulawesi
65028918B17554737605304.summary:
In April 2025 Makassar's mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral; the deputy chair of the DPRD's legislation body, Anwar Faruq, backed it as urgently needed "to preserve moral order and religious norms." South Sulawesi is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight International's discriminatory-regulation mapping. No enacted local bylaw with specified penalties yet exists in the province, and no violence wave or mass police raid against trans people is documented in the dossier.

The small negative deviation from the national score reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway to eastern Indonesia, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement. It remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles specifying fines and rehabilitation is already on the books, and above Jakarta (0.12), where a 56-person raid without legal basis has already occurred: the law here is proposed, not enacted, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule the traveler-facing impact is prospective.

For this record: documents formal municipal push in Makassar toward an anti-LGBT regulation in 2025.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces - South Sulawesi among them - documenting how provincial and city bylaws criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under regional autonomy.

DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families, and DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting showing rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement. This is a dated, Makassar-city-specific record of the administrative track of the anti-LGBT push the record describes, confirming that as of April 2026 the local rule remains proposed (Ranperda) rather than enacted.

Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti calls such raperdas a 'trend ahead of the political year' that risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people, and notes the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations. This verifies Makassar as a recurring site of the anti-LGBT bylaw push since at least early 2023, predating the April 2025 mayoral reaffirmation the record cites, and consistent with its 'proposed, not enacted' status.

65028918B9551391119865.name: South Sumatra
65028918B9551391119865.summary:
On 19 July 2026 Palembang's city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation (Perpres) No. 111 of 2025 on the national defence policy 2025-2029, which lists the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats; Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. The regulation remains in preparation, not enacted, with no specified penalty; no enforcement event is documented for this province. South Sumatra is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight's discriminatory-regulation mapping, and its neighbour Lampung saw a documented Satpol PP raid on three transwomen (November 2018) - the Sumatran belt is where local enforcement is consolidating.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT measures from moral panic to national-defence doctrine - the August 2026 ABC reporting links the 'rule that deems them a threat' to a wave of street attacks on trans women, though it cautions the trend cannot yet be confirmed - but without an enacted local penalty the traveler-facing risk here remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions.

31927357B17004778023462.name: Aguascalientes
31927357B17004778023462.summary:
Aguascalientes sits under the national framework: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or trans presence, while legal gender recognition nationally remains a state-by-state mosaic that the national courts have pressed legislatures to complete. No state-level recognition law, no hostile ordinances and no state-specific enforcement or incident series is documented in the surviving audited sources.

The one state-specific legal development is the national supreme court's April 2026 ruling that the state's civil-code requirements for changing the gender marker on birth certificates — judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations — are discriminatory and violate privacy; the court ordered the state's civil registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, with a new birth certificate issued and no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate effect is limited to persons represented by the civil association that filed it, so the general position for a transgender visitor is unchanged: no enacted recognition procedure covering the general public, and no documented incidents in the surviving sources.

They state trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression, and cite the ENDISEG survey showing 7.3% of the state's population aged 15+ self-identifies as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among Mexican states. This is the first state-specific documentation for this record of ongoing anti-trans violence and family rejection in Aguascalientes beyond the absence of a recognition law.

sources.summary: Zeta Tijuana (8 July 2023, Rosario Mosso Castro) reports that Brayan Rivera was presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson in provisional detention for extradition, accused by Mexico of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in room 404 of Hotel Cascadas beside Bar Hong Kong in Tijuana's tolerance zone; probable cause was determined on 29 June 2023 by the US federal court, and he was arrested at his parents' Downey, California home, where officers found the Hotel Cascadas rent receipt and rope and gloves. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Colima, and no law targets trans presence. sources.summary: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state-by-state — as of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists (identity-document mismatch driving discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco). For this record: the national mosaic, not any locally enacted certainty, is the operative framework.

HRW/Community Center for Inclusion report (6 Mar 2024) on a Mexican state lacking a legal gender-recognition procedure, documented in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries violence, harassment and humiliation risk, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions; context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. For this record it is the operative evidence of what 'state law silent' means for trans people on the ground.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years — the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it, after Nayarit (up to 60 years). In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, with transfemicide impunity thought higher still. For this record: benchmarks the national lethality level and the emerging transfemicide-crime trend under which the region sits.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
For a visitor, the state's position is no-recognition: as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists, so identity documents issued in Tamaulipas cannot be changed through any administrative route, and mismatched documents invite exactly the police checks and institutional mistreatment that a companion 2024 report documents in one such state - the daily-interaction risk that most endangers a visible trans visitor.

On protections, the congress of the state unanimously approved, on 18 June 2025, reforms to the local Penal Code adding a chapter covering crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression and explicitly banning 'conversion therapies', with prison terms of 2-6 years and fines of up to 2,000 times a local measurement unit; the penalties increase by half when victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or in family, medical or workplace settings. For practical safety, the documented armed-group targeting and extortion of trans women along the border is the trans-specific danger driver, against blanket border violence that affects every traveller regardless of gender expression.

sources.summary: On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups (including Tamaulipas Diversidad, Vihda Trans A.C., Tendremos Alas A.C. and La Resistencia Trans) agreed a joint agenda to push a Gender Identity Law and anti-discrimination and health reforms, noting the initiatives have been pending since June 2025 and that the absent law keeps limiting trans people's access to health, education and employment. Confirms that as of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and a Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.

31927357B22008724034476.name: Tlaxcala
31927357B22008724034476.summary:
For a trans visitor to Tlaxcala, the operative facts are documents and the legal floor: an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition exists via the state's 2019 reform of the Civil Code (Decree D.113, dated 1 October 2019), with no court proceeding; the national Supreme Court's 17 October 2018 ruling makes name and gender-marker change available through a simple administrative procedure based on self-declaration; and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the final states completed legalisation in 2022.

No jurisdiction-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; Mexico's national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country. A March 2025 count by Human Rights Watch places the jurisdiction among the 22 of 32 state units that have legislated a gender-recognition procedure — not among the six that have enacted none.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
For a trans visitor to Yucatán the operative document fact is recent: the state's 2024 reform of the Civil Registry Law (publication in the official gazette on 26 April 2024) created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, placing the jurisdiction among Mexican state units that offer an administrative — rather than court-ordered — route to update legal gender on documents. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count likewise places it among the 22 of 32 states with a legislated procedure, not among the six without one.

Marriage equality is settled: same-sex marriage was secured through court rulings from July 2013 and codified by the state's September 2021 constitutional amendment and 1 March 2022 secondary legislation; a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban has been in effect since 25 August 2021. No jurisdiction-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern against transgender people is supported by the surviving sources; the national criminal and human-rights framework applies in the state as elsewhere in Mexico.

The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022, and Yucatán is listed as enacting a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, still in effect alongside the state bans from Mexico City (31 July 2020) and elsewhere. The page also records the federal framework: same-sex acts decriminalised since 1871, tolerance of sexual diversity documented among Yucatán Maya groups, and the conversion-therapy ban passed federally by the Chamber of Deputies in March 2023 (267-104) after a 69-16 Senate vote in October 2022.

31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
For a trans visitor to Zacatecas the document route is recent and explicit: a December 2022 reform of the state's Family Code — approved by the 64th Legislature with 14 votes in favour and 7 against — establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community, and Human Rights Watch's March 2025 feature records the same reform as an administrative procedure, with the Civil Registry director's 2023 implementing guidelines.

A protective criminal-law floor applies: since 25 August 2021 the state Penal Code prohibits and sanctions conversion therapies, penalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression with one to three years' imprisonment or community work, and the same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. The jurisdiction is not among the six Mexican state units without a legislated gender-recognition procedure per Human Rights Watch's March 2025 count (22 of 32). No jurisdiction-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern targeting transgender people appears in the surviving sources; the national criminal law and gender-recognition regime apply here as elsewhere in the country.

sources.title: Diputados aprueban reforma en beneficio de la comunidad trans (La Jornada Zacatecas)
sources.summary: La Jornada Zacatecas, 23 December 2022, reports that with 14 votes in favour and 7 against, deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved the reform of the Family Code of the State of Zacatecas on gender identity, establishing the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community; the Justice Committee had already issued a positive opinion (dictamen) on the reform. This is the local record of the 2022 enactment against which this record's central claim — that Zacatecas is not among the states lacking a legislated gender-recognition procedure — is checked. Page verified via the Wayback Machine snapshot of 7 October 2025; the live ljz.mx URL is Cloudflare-blocked (HTTP 403).

sources.title: ¡Eso! Zacatecas prohíbe las terapias de conversión o los ECOSIG (Sopitas)
sources.summary: Sopitas, 30 August 2021, reports that on 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved prohibiting and sanctioning conversion therapies or 'ECOSIG' (Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género) by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code — penalised with one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work against anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or promotes such practices; the same session also typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code. The article further records that the gender-identity law initiative debated alongside (constitutional and family-code reform) failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending at the time — the reform only passed in December 2022. Documents the protective state-level criminal-law floor applying in Zacatecas, with an explicit ban on practices aimed at changing gender identity.

82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
For a trans visitor to Newfoundland and Labrador the local legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law, enforcement pattern or official statement was found; criminal law and the national human-rights framework apply uniformly, and the jurisdiction has no facility or expression rule differing from the national position. The documented risk signals are weak — police-reported hate crime is the lowest in the country (5.3 per 100,000 in 2024) — and risk is assessed at parity with the national picture.

Documents: the province's sex-designation change requires birth in the province or three months' residence, operates without any surgery requirement and without an application fee, and the province states it cannot guarantee that an 'X' gender marker on its documents will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the caveat that matters for a visitor carrying provincial records while travelling; the 2016 amendment also removed the surgery requirement for changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023, after a +34% jump in 2023); national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents.

sources.title: Changes to Vital Statistics Act Would Allow for Change of Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.summary: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 17 June 2021: proposed changes to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 would allow residents of the province who were not born there — but have lived there at least three months — to change their sex designation; the change certificate carries a $25 fee, counts as official provincial identification and 'could be leveraged by the applicant to update records in other jurisdictions,' serving as the identification document for people born outside the country. The release states the amendments align with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading that day and Royal Assent on 23 June 2021. Gives the province a resident-based legal gender-change route (three-month residency) relevant to document enrolment for trans people in Newfoundland and Labrador.

sources.title: Legislative Amendment Respects Rights of Transgender Individuals (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.summary: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 12 April 2016: an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 removes the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission (the December 2015 ruling on complaints from two trans women) and with LGBTQ advocates' requests. The province's gender-marker change on provincial records has therefore operated without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment (Royal Assent 13 April 2016).

sources.title: Changing Your Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador)
sources.summary: Current official Government of Newfoundland and Labrador page: applicants for a change of sex designation must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s (with consent of the other parent/guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15), and must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months; there is no fee for the change application, with charges applying only to official copies of updated documents (new birth certificate $35, or $30 online). The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate with an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the documented cross-border document caveat relevant to carrying provincial records elsewhere.

sources.title: P.E.I. transgender community applauds ID changes (CBC News)
sources.summary: CBC News, 18 April 2016, reports that the MacLauchlan government tabled a bill to amend the Vital Statistics Act so Islanders can change their gender on official documents by declaring the gender they identify with plus a letter from a doctor, with sex-reassignment surgery no longer required; Pride P.E.I. board member Jesse Macmillan welcomed the move, noting surgery is expensive and the closest provider was in Montreal, and called for a future third gender category, adding that many of his friends in Charlottetown identify outside the binary; a linked item on the article page reports Health PEI would cover the costs of three surgeries for transgender patients. PEI's gender-marker change on provincial documents has worked without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment.

sources.title: Improving diversity and inclusion on driver's licences (Government of Prince Edward Island news release)
sources.summary: Government of Prince Edward Island news release, 30 November 2018: Islanders may now select 'gender not listed' (shown on the licence as X) or 'prefer not to say' (blank) alongside male and female when identifying gender on a driver's licence; the release states PEI is the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say'/blank option, quoting Transportation, Infrastructure and Energy Minister Paula Biggar and PEERS Alliance. The change took effect 4 December 2018 at Access PEI locations, meaning provincial photo ID can carry an X or blank gender marker.

sources.title: Change of Gender Designation (Government of Prince Edward Island)
sources.summary: Official Government of PEI information page (content as captured in the Wayback Machine snapshot of 1 July 2022; the live page is bot-gated): an adult may apply for a change of gender designation if born in PEI and resident in the province for at least three months and not in the lawful custody of another person; a legal custodian may apply for a minor under 18 who was born on PEI and has lived in the province at least three months, with written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if aged 12 or older. The application requires completed forms including a physician statement, a written statement by the applicant, and signature arranged before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics — a provincial gender-marker regime operating without a surgery requirement and with physician attestation.

82249235B69645938038492.name: Nova Scotia
82249235B69645938038492.summary:
For a trans visitor to Nova Scotia the legal floor is quiet: no jurisdiction-specific trans law or hostile official pattern was found; federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly. The capital hosts a large, organised 2SLGBTQ+ community with institutional support, while the documented national hostility pattern elsewhere concentrates in other provinces' school-board and library politics — not this jurisdiction. Outside the capital, expect the rural small-town profile national surveys find worse for trans and non-binary people. Risk broadly at parity with the national picture.

The one enforcement signal on record is a custodial case: a trans woman from the capital region is challenging the decision to hold her in a men's correctional facility while she serves a two-year sentence; a federal judge gave her more time to file for judicial review, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers that restricted her access to her lawyer (18 March 2025) — the documented case shows how a trans woman's correctional placement is being challenged and judicially reviewed in the jurisdiction's custodial system.

sources.title: N.S. transgender prisoner looking to challenge decision to hold her in men's prison - Saltwire / The Chronicle Herald
sources.summary: The Chronicle Herald reports (18 March 2025) that a federal judge gave a transgender woman from the Halifax region more time to file her application for judicial review of the decision to hold her in a men's prison while she serves a two-year robbery sentence; the judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted the applicant's access to her lawyer. sources.title: Grants to Support 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Groups, Provincial Conference - Government of Nova Scotia
sources.summary: The Government of Nova Scotia announced (10 June 2026) more than $176,000 through the first round of its new 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, with awards including $25,000 to Pictou County Pride, $25,000 to LakeCity Works' Queer Careers program in Dartmouth and $12,067 to SeaHorse Sexual Health Centre for queer and trans outreach on the Eastern Shore, plus $50,000 to Truro Pride to host the province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference; per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year. This is official, dated evidence of provincial funding and institutional support for 2SLGBTQIA+ communities across Nova Scotia.

sources.title: Province Releases First 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan - Government of Nova Scotia

This is official confirmation that Nova Scotia operates an explicit provincial inclusion framework rather than restrictive trans-specific legislation.

sources.title: Gender Identity Protected by the Quebec Charter of Rights - Éducaloi
sources.summary: Éducaloi reports that on 10 June 2024 Quebec's Human Rights Tribunal found a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training; the page notes gender identity and expression were added as prohibited grounds of discrimination under Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms in 2016, and cites 2021 census data that 0.14% of Quebecers aged 15 and older (0.27% of those aged 15-34) identify as transgender. sources.title: 'Parents must be fully involved' in student's decision to change pronouns, Ontario education minister says - CTV News
sources.summary: CTV News reports (28 August 2023) that Ontario's education minister, Stephen Lecce, said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronouns at school, speaking the same week Saskatchewan joined New Brunswick in legislating parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names and pronouns; Lecce added that teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child, and Ontario did not adopt such legislation at that time. The article documents the Ontario government's stance on pronoun and name rules in schools at the peak of the 2023 Canadian pronoun-policy wave - the province held the line against legislating parental consent.

sources.title: Policy on preventing discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression - Ontario Human Rights Commission
sources.summary: The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations; it defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

sources.title: Manitoba government eyes human rights protection for gender expression - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.summary: Global News Winnipeg (18 March 2025) reports the Manitoba NDP government plans to expand the province's Human Rights Code to cover gender expression - the code already prohibits discrimination based on gender identity, and Justice Minister Matt Wiebe says the change would bring Manitoba in line with most other provinces and cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The amendment sits in a government bill before the legislature, to be debated later in 2025, and is welcomed by Charlie Eau, executive director of Trans Manitoba. This is the first province-specific human-rights-protection development on record for Manitoba, filling the gap the record notes for provincial-level trans law and official statements.

sources.title: Bill to mark transgender and two-spirit day passed by Manitoba legislature - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.summary: Global News Winnipeg (30 May 2024) reports the Manitoba legislature passed a bill recognizing March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a backbench New Democrat MLA for Kirkfield Park who is transgender. Oxenham said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported. The Legislative Assembly's passage gives Manitoba a dated, legislatively enacted trans-specific recognition at provincial level.

sources.title: Manitoba reaffirms support for trans community on Day of Remembrance - Global News (Winnipeg)
sources.summary: Global News Winnipeg (20 Nov 2023) reports Manitoba again raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance - an observance the province first marked eight years earlier - this time with the flag raised by Logan Oxenham, the first openly trans man elected to the Manitoba legislature. In a statement, families minister Nahanni Fontaine and health minister Uzoma Asagwara said the government 'supports and upholds the life-saving work' of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse Manitobans, and Brandon advocate Anastasia Gibson said the day memorializes people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing. This documents Manitoba's official provincial position on trans people with dates, named officials and a local advocacy voice.

sources.title: RCMP raise concerns over name change notification in NWT legislation - Cabin Radio
sources.summary: Cabin Radio (2 June 2026) reports the NWT Legislative Assembly is taking feedback from police and the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and Change of Name Act to make the legislation 'more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people', including an option for trans and non-binary people to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. 14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary:
England is where the national law applies without a devolved layer: no regional administration exists, and the national equality institutions and courts sit principally here. The decisive recent ruling for trans visitors is the decision of 16 April 2025 by the country's highest court (the national Supreme Court), which settled that 'sex' and 'woman' in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological or registered sex, and that an acquired gender certificate does not change legal sex for equality-law purposes. That definition is the ground on which services, searches and detention allocation operate for anyone detained here.

Operative enforcement guidance: after the ruling the national equality body updated its code of practice (May 2025) advising that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is 'genuine concern' about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport 'when necessary' for safety — the guidance a visitor meets at venues, transport and services day to day.

Practical-safety baseline: police-recorded hate crime in England and Wales (year ending March 2025) stood at 115,990 incidents, with the transgender strand down 11% year on year; recorded figures understate prevalence, and a February 2024 recording-system change means earlier years over-counted.

sources.summary: BBC News (19 June 2026): a judge (Lady Ross, Court of Session) ruled Scottish Prison Service guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity unlawful — sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 'definition of a woman' ruling. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same UK-wide ruling imposes on England's prison and custody decisions; the first minister said the government will consider the judgment (the Supreme Court had already held Article 8 confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation).

BBC News (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary:
Queensland is assessed on the national framework: same-sex conduct was decriminalised here in the 1990s reforms, and rights have broadly advanced in line with the national standard since then. Two state-specific protective mechanisms are now confirmed on the record: a criminal ban on conversion practices (enacted August 2020, the first in the country), and an anti-discrimination rewrite (commenced 29 April 2024) that modernises the gender-identity attribute, extends protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and moves serious vilification into the criminal code with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment.

Adverse state-level mechanism also on file: since January 2025 new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria are barred from puberty blockers and hormone therapy under a health-directive regime that exempts existing patients; the measure is legally contested and has been characterised as making the state an outlier. No visitor documents, border-screening practice or marriage/partner-travel consequence specific to this state is recorded, so a visitor stands under the national baseline while weighing the confirmed protections and the confirmed youth-health restriction together.

This confirms the record's second headline claim - the 2024 anti-discrimination rewrite modernising the gender-identity attribute - citing the Queensland Human Rights Commission's own statement, and replaces the state page that was unreachable at audit.

sources.title: The Ongoing Fight Against Queensland's Trans Youth Healthcare Ban - Star Observer
sources.summary: Star Observer reports (4 February 2026) that Queensland's Health Minister Tim Nicholls halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria in January 2025, formalised by a 28 January 2025 Queensland Health directive that exempts existing Queensland Children's Gender Service patients; Equality Australia called Queensland an 'outlier state', and the ban remains legally contested, with affected families reporting private treatment costs of hundreds of dollars per injection (nearly $2,000 in one case). This is a confirmed Queensland-specific adverse health-access measure in effect for the current visit window - the kind of local mechanism the audited record said was absent.

82085004B14973555098025.name: South Australia
82085004B14973555098025.summary:
South Australia carries no region-specific incident series or enforcement pattern in the dossier, but the current-status record documents a protective state-level framework a visitor stands under: since 2017 the sex descriptor on a state birth certificate can be changed with appropriate clinical treatment and without surgery or forced divorce, with non-binary and 'indeterminate' descriptors available — among the first two national units to allow change without surgery. Hate-crime sentencing law explicitly covers sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status (implemented November 2021), and a conversion-practices prohibition has been in legal effect since April 2025.

Relationships and partner travel: registered domestic relationships exist (from August 2017) and same-sex marriage has been legal since December 2017 under the national law. The one operational divergence still differing from some neighbours: custody placement is not on the explicit self-identification basis used by several other states, so a detained trans woman's placement depends on surgical-intervention status or case-by-case assessment.

Nothing adverse on visitor documents or border screening is recorded; neither a protective nor a hostile state-level campaign beyond the statutes above is documented.

14911670B45290909693812.summary:
The national framework applies in Roraima with no documented state-level deviation for a visitor: protections are judicial rather than statutory - name and gender-marker change without surgery or court order under the national court's 2018 ruling, discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under the 2019 ruling, and marriage and adoption long settled by the national courts - with non-binary birth-certificate recognition handled case-by-case, varying state by state.

The country as a whole records the world's highest absolute toll of killings of trans people, concentrated away from the capitals, and observers stress that protections are uneven in practice, thinning in the interior; for a visitor the picture is the national one with an interior discount - rights on paper, thin services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility mechanism on record either way.

sources.summary: Country-framework page (revised through 2026): same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. The framework that governs it shifted sharply in March 2026: parliament passed an amendment removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinnar) and intersex people, and mandating medical certification for identity documents and for surgery; the medical-certification mandate is a direct documents consequence for a trans traveler whose papers now rest on that certification, and the change bears uniformly on every state and union territory, so it reaches visitors identically.

Practical safety: a nationally recurring policing practice treats trans appearance as a suspicion category in transit spaces, evidenced by an August 2024 railway-platform groping complaint — a formal complaint was filed and intrusive questioning reported — reaching visitors through federal transport policing rather than any local law.

sources.summary: The 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill amends the 2019 law: it removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted categories and intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition - HRW calls it a major reversal of the 2014 rights and urges the president not to sign it (articles dated 26 Mar 2026).

Amendment bill approved by both houses (article 2026, awaiting presidential assent): removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court 'third gender' ruling; narrows the 2019 definition of transgender person; government says the narrower definition improves welfare delivery, critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people; mandatory medical certification described as an attack on privacy and dignity.

1811400B15456792557830.name: Sikkim
1811400B15456792557830.summary:
No Sikkim-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file; the state sits under the national framework, which narrowed sharply in March 2026: parliament removed the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricted recognition to intersex variations and traditional community identities certified by medical boards, and made medical-board certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery — so identity-document and surgery-authorisation practice for a trans traveler now rests on board certification. A court-appointed advisory panel asked for withdrawal, prominent trans activists warned of mass exclusion, protests followed the vote, and assent is pending.

The framework's enforcement texture nationally includes transit-space 'gender checks': an August 2024 case at a northern railway station, in which a trans traveller alleged a rail-police constable groped her while checking her gender — police denied it and filed a counter-complaint — evidencing a policing habit of treating trans appearance as suspicion in federally policed transit spaces rather than in this state specifically.

The national framework governs recognition here, and the March 2026 amendment narrows it: both houses of parliament passed the amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons Act that removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricts legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinner) and intersex people — excluding self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people — and requires medical certification for identity recognition, with medical boards and district authorities certifying gender-affirming surgery; human-rights reporting adds a new offence carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026. Recognition is already thin in practice: only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons — a small fraction — hold identity cards.

No Mizoram-specific trans statute or enforcement record is on file; neither international reporting on the change nor any other source on file records Mizoram-level deviation — statute, ban, or enforcement campaign — in either direction. The northeast state’s day-to-day exposure for a trans visitor therefore runs through the central framework, its pending narrowing included.

sources.summary: HRW report (26 Mar 2026): India's parliament passed the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill narrowing the 2019 law: it removes self-identification, restricts legal recognition to traditionally recognised groups (hijra/kinner) and intersex persons, and requires medical certification for identity recognition — reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling. The bill adds offences including up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' anyone to be transgender, which HRW warns could criminalise support networks. Of 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. HRW urges the president not to sign; assent pending as of late March 2026.

BBC (26 Mar 2026): India's parliament passed an amendment to the 2019 transgender-rights law replacing self-identification with recognition based on biological or physical traits plus traditional identities (hijra/kinner-style); medical boards and district authorities must now certify gender-affirming surgery. The government says the narrower definition targets welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling; presidential assent is pending. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

1811400B56841107211215.name: Karnātaka
1811400B56841107211215.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier: the country-level research identified no Karnataka-specific enforcement series or incident pattern material enough to score separately (±0.02), so it is assessed at the national score. For a trans visitor the national framework is the operative baseline: the March 2026 amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons Act, passed by both houses of parliament, removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricts legal recognition to historically recognised socio-cultural groups (hijra, kinner) plus intersex people — excluding self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people — and requires medical certification for identity recognition, with medical boards and district authorities certifying gender-affirming surgery; it also adds a new offence carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

Recognition in practice is thin: of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons, only about 32,500 — a small fraction — hold identity cards, so a trans visitor’s documentation position on the ground is uneven.

Framework item for German Länder, incl. Baden-Württemberg: Verfassungsblog analysis (18 Mar 2026) of prison placement for trans prisoners. Placement rules in most Länder were unchanged since the 1970s and are being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of Rhineland-Palatinate's prison law is in force, with Bavarian, Saxon and Hamburg rules also recently entering into force — giving a majority of Länder revised rules. The piece argues there is no constitutional duty to anchor placement to the registered gender entry (a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination), and notes only Bremen's law explicitly references the gender entry while others do so implicitly. Baden-Württemberg is not named: its own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules.

sources.summary: The North Rhine-Westphalian state ministry page records that on 25 April 2025 the Land government published the study „Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*“, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans*, inter*, queer and non-binary people (LSBTIQ*) in the Land. 25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
This region is assessed at the national score: the dedicated country dossier identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02). A visitor stands under the national trans-equality law of 28 February 2023, which applies uniformly across the autonomous communities: adults rectify the registered sex marker by simple declaration with no medical diagnosis or treatment requirement and corresponding document adaptation, LGBTI non-discrimination protections extend to healthcare, employment and housing, and recognition from age 12 is available under conditions.

The regional base is permissive rather than restrictive: gender self-declaration has been possible since 2021, a gender-identity non-discrimination law has stood since 2014, and the region is listed among communities banning conversion therapies, so the national framework layers onto regional practice; parts of the region are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. For partner travel, the national law provides parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples; no region-specific marriage provision is recorded.

sources.summary: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023 (BOE no. 51, 1 March 2023), the 'Law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGBTI persons' (the 'Trans Law'), applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: Title II allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration, with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, and provides for corresponding document adaptation. The law further mandates public-policy, workplace, health and education measures, and its transitory provisions govern rectification applications pending at entry into force.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) reports the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The same law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 can obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. HRW places the reform within European and international standards against disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Spain (Wikipedia): Canary Islands — same-sex registry 2003, gender-identity non-discrimination law 2014, gender self-declaration since 2021
sources.summary: The English Wikipedia page 'LGBTQ rights in Spain' covers the Canary Islands specifically in its autonomous-community sections: the community created its same-sex couple registry in 2003; it was among the first to ban employment and other discrimination on gender-identity grounds via Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 (non-discrimination on gender-identity grounds and recognition of trans persons' rights, BOE-A-2014-11995); and it has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 communities doing so before the national Ley Trans of 28 February 2023. The Canary Islands are also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. For a trans traveler the region therefore stands under a regional anti-discrimination and self-identification regime layered on the 2023 national law this record already cites.

sources.title: Historia LGBT en el País Vasco (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Spanish Wikipedia's dedicated article on LGBT history in the Basque Country: the Basque Parliament passed a specific law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people (the page dates it to 2013) and for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system; earlier institutional markers are the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. Region-specific confirmation that the Basque Country runs its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions (Emakunde) under the national framework — the divergence-vs-framework question this record addresses.

sources.title: BOE-A-2016-6170 — Ley 8/2016, de 27 de mayo, de igualdad social de lesbianas, gais, bisexuales, transexuales, transgénero e intersexuales, y de políticas públicas contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género en la Comunidad Autónoma de la Región de Murcia (BOE)
sources.summary: Official gazette text of the Region of Murcia's own LGTBI-equality statute beneath the national framework, confirming this record's claim that regional LGTBI legislation exists for Murcia. Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170) prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics in public and private activity in the region, and within its scope bars any requirement to prove declared gender identity by psychological or medical report. Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation/consultation body in which LGTBI entities are represented. Title IV sets a sanctioning ladder: minor breaches a warning or fine of up to €3,000; serious breaches €3,001–€20,000 (including degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI persons or their families in the provision of services); very serious breaches €20,001–€45,000, with accessory penalties such as exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year; multiple discrimination raises the infraction grade.

sources.summary: Official gazette text of Catalonia's own LGTBI-rights statute, Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014 (Generalitat de Catalunya; DOGC núm. 6730, 17 October 2014), the autonomous law after which the 2010s wave of Spanish regional LGTBI laws followed. It defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects gender identity. It extends protections across education, health, employment and sport (including broadening the Observatorio Catalán del Deporte to action against violence and discrimination in sport) and guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects. Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiencia de Catalunya (between seven days' and three months' worth); Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, with the Síndic de Greuges able to instigate proceedings.

sources.title: Derechos LGBT en España (Spanish Wikipedia, national framework context)
sources.summary: Framework-context source naming this jurisdiction: the national article records two Catalonia-firsts inside the Spanish framework — the 30 June 1998 Ley de Parejas of Catalonia, which it calls the first Spanish couples law allowing homosexual couples minimum legal provisions, and the Generalitat de Catalunya's 2014 law (Ley 11/2014) that prompted the 2010s wave of autonomous LGTBI laws — the basis of this record's treatment of the region as the national front-runner. It also dates the state framework governing the region: same-sex marriage since 2 July 2005, the 2007 gender-identity law, and the Ley 4/2023 trans law approved in February 2023 (registered sex change from age 16 without medical reports or hormonal treatment), whose implementation falls to the regional government. Operative regional instrument: Ley 11/2014 de Cataluña.

25490228B80227492032103.modelContext: Barcelona: world-class scene, city-level protections, vast tourism envelope; Catalan institutions explicitly protective.
25490228B80227492032103.blindSummary:
A visitor to this region stands under the national framework in force across the autonomous communities: the 2023 national trans-equality law allows adults to rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration without prior medical diagnosis or treatment and provides for corresponding document adaptation, and same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2 July 2005, so marriage and partner-travel carry full legal effect. The law also prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing and enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples.

Practical safety is comparatively favourable on the record: no region-specific adverse incident, ordinance or enforcement finding was identified for this region in the country dossier, no sub-national facility, expression or assembly restriction exists anywhere in the country, and the region contains one of the country's densest, most visible LGBTI urban centres with dedicated hate-crime structures within its own regional police force. The national victimisation baseline nonetheless applies — a 2026 national report found 44% of LGBTI respondents had experienced a hate-motivated incident — with the dossier's fault line being city-versus-rural rather than region-versus-region.
blindSourceSummaries: Official gazette text of the national trans-equality law of 28 February 2023, applying uniformly across the autonomous communities: adults may rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, with corresponding document adaptation and mandated public-policy, workplace, health and education measures.

An international rights organisation reports the passage of the national trans law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment; the law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, prohibits discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, and lets children from age 12 obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious.

Official gazette text of this region's own LGBTI-rights statute of 10 October 2014, the autonomous law after which the 2010s wave of regional LGBTI laws followed: it defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, obliges regional public administrations to make administrative documentation reflect gender identity, extends protections across education, health, employment and sport, guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures, and places a sanctioning regime under the department competent for non-discrimination with an oversight body able to instigate proceedings.

National-framework context: the national article records two region-firsts inside the national framework — a 1998 regional couples law called the first in the country allowing homosexual couples minimum legal provisions, and the region's 2014 law that prompted the 2010s wave of autonomous LGBTI laws — and dates the framework: same-sex marriage since 2 July 2005, the 2007 gender-identity law, and the 2023 trans law approved in February 2023, whose implementation falls to the regional government.

25490228B94630301010512.name: Castilla-La Mancha
25490228B94630301010512.summary:
A visitor to this region stands under the national position, which governs because the country dossier identified nothing region-specific: no facility, expression or assembly restriction exists at sub-national level anywhere in the country, the 2023 national trans-equality law is implemented by the regional government, and the national victimisation baseline applies — a 2026 federation report found 44% of LGBTI respondents had experienced a hate-motivated incident.

Document-relevant provision is national: adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment, the right to the registered change being grounded in the free development of personality, and the international rights organisation's account of the reform confirms recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process replacing the previous gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years' medical treatment requirements; the law also protects unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing.

sources.summary: State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the national 'Trans Law' for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, applies uniformly across Spain's autonomous communities, including this one: adults may rectify the registered sex entry without prior surgical reassignment, the right to the registered change being grounded in the free development of personality (art. 10.1 CE). The law further defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances - the national framework the regional position in this record rests on.

Human Rights Watch (16 February 2023) on the Spanish Congress's passage of the national Trans Law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the previous gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment requirements; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious. The law also strengthens protections for unmarried same-sex couples and combats LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. These are the national provisions this autonomous community implements under the same framework.
