19177384B51705615570562.name: Mendoza
19177384B51705615570562.summary:
No Mendoza-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented for transgender visitors; interior divisions without local reporting infrastructure generate few records even where risk is real, and the country-wide security picture for trans and travesti people has sharply deteriorated. A visitor therefore stands under the national framework: the February 2025 roll-back of the gender-identity framework restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and an April 2025 national feature described the transgender community as facing a 'chaotic, desperate situation' amid the current national administration's policies.

Practical safety: the national hate-crime observatory recorded at least 227 attacks motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — up 62% year on year, the highest figure of its decade of operation, roughly one every 38 hours — with perpetrators predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, beatings the main modality. Attacks continued into early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of the president of an LGBTIQ+ organisation in a northern province.

sources.summary: April 2025 Washington Blade dateline Buenos Aires: national framework binding this province - the Feb 5, 2025 decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments; the 1% Trans Labor Quota hires were dismissed and federal anti-discrimination agency INADI abolished in 2024; activists told the Blade police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common under Milei, explicitly worse "even more so" in interior provinces without strong reporting infrastructure.

Agencia Presentes (19 Mar 2026) on the national hate-crime observatory record: 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina in 2025 - up 62% year on year, a ten-year record, one every 38 hours; perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, beatings the main modality, institutional violence up from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), 32% of 2025 incidents in police stations or prisons, and 43% of perpetrators strangers to their victims. This province sits under that national picture with no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

Milei's Feb 5 2025 decree restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgeries and hormone treatments. The 2012 Gender Identity Law (legal gender change without medical intervention, 'X' DNI marker since 2021) remains formally in force but is no longer guaranteed, activists report.

The same period saw DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatments.

19177384B64043309462999.name: Río Negro
19177384B64043309462999.summary:
The provincial statute reserving at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people — one of only a handful of provinces with such a law — signals a provincial official posture better than the national baseline, though the surveys reviewed found none of these quota laws actually being complied with.

For a visitor the operative exposure is the national one: the contravención/faltas (police infraction) powers remain, and the February 2025 national decrees curtailing the Gender Identity Law (minors' transition treatments; prison placement of trans detainees) apply here too. Because national trans-death counts are small enough that one provincial case is a real signal, the 2024 national MuMaLa registry entry attributing a travesti victim to this province (jointly with a neighbouring province) counts as a local risk signal.

Frame applies to this province as part of the national position.

17162690B9130125042960.name: Lower Silesian Voivodeship
17162690B9130125042960.summary:
This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score, and the national framework is what a trans traveler stands under here. For a visitor the operative enforcement-relevant standards are detention-side: national law bars placing a person in a guarded centre wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence, and the framework was exercised in practice on 13 March 2024, when a court placed a transgender foreign woman (on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners, the border guard initially refused to move or release her despite the legal bar, and she was released only after a legal-aid association's application to the border-guard post commander.

On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that denying hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman in prison violated her right to private and family life and awarded damages, holding the refusal disproportionate with no reasonable legal grounds; the judgment binds the whole country and governs prison and detention healthcare in every voivodeship, including this one. No division-specific incident series, hostility mechanism or enforcement pattern is documented, so the visitor reads the national position without a local added risk factor.

sources.summary: Case report (Association for Legal Intervention, 13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman who had been on hormone therapy since 2018 in a guarded centre for male foreigners, and the Border Guard refused to move or release her despite Polish law barring placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence. After the association's application to the Border Guard Post commander she was released (page updated 28 Mar 2024). Establishes the current framework for trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention - directly relevant to any trans visitor detained while in this voivodeship.

ECtHR ruling coverage (TGEU, 16 Jul 2024): on 11 Jul 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life (Article 8 ECHR) by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 damages; the Court left the alleged Articles 3 and 14 breaches undecided but held the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment is binding on Poland as a whole - the governing standard for trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including this one.

For a visitor the operative enforcement-relevant standards are detention-side: national law bars placing a person in a guarded centre wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence, and the framework was exercised in practice on 13 March 2024, when a court placed a transgender foreign woman (on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners, the border guard initially refused to move or release her despite the legal bar, and she was released only after a legal-aid association's application to the border-guard post commander.

On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that denying hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman in prison violated her right to private and family life and awarded damages, holding the refusal disproportionate with no reasonable legal grounds; the judgment binds the whole country and governs prison and detention healthcare in every voivodeship, including this one. No division-specific incident series, hostility mechanism or enforcement pattern is documented, so the visitor reads the national position without a local added risk factor.

sources.summary: Case report (Association for Legal Intervention, 13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman who had been on hormone therapy since 2018 in a guarded centre for male foreigners, and the Border Guard refused to move or release her despite Polish law barring placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence. After the association's application to the Border Guard Post commander she was released (page updated 28 Mar 2024). Establishes the current framework for trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention - directly relevant to any trans visitor detained while in this voivodeship.

ECtHR ruling coverage (TGEU, 16 Jul 2024): on 11 Jul 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life (Article 8 ECHR) by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 damages; the Court left the alleged Articles 3 and 14 breaches undecided but held the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment is binding on Poland as a whole - the governing standard for trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including this one.

17162690B77437931625010.name: Pomeranian Voivodeship
17162690B77437931625010.summary: No voivodeship-level trans-specific resolution, incident series or enforcement finding was located for this division in the current research pass. The anti-LGBT municipal-resolution wave (80+ municipalities and four voivodeship-level declarations as of March 2020) concentrated in the eastern and south-eastern parts of the country, so the absence of local findings here indicates thinner documentation rather than established safety. The national frame governs this division: no hate-crime protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (the March 2025 amendment bill referred to the Constitutional Tribunal, hearings held July and September 2025), court-based and medically gatekept legal gender recognition, and national sources documenting a trans foreign woman held in a male-only guarded detention centre and an ECtHR ruling that denying a prisoner hormone therapy violates private life.

sources.summary: Association for Legal Intervention (13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender woman (Vietnamese citizen, on hormone therapy since 2018) in a guarded centre for male foreigners; Border Guard refused to move/release her despite her identifying as a woman and warning that stopping medication would harm her. After an intervention by the legal-aid organisation citing Polish law, court rulings and international standards, the Border Guard Commander released her because continued detention there posed a serious health risk. Useful to this record: in Poland, detained foreign trans women face placement in male-only facilities until formally challenged, and release can depend on legal intervention.

TGEU, 16 Jul 2024: on 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (right to private and family life) of the ECHR by denying a trans woman access to hormone replacement therapy while imprisoned, despite her having been prescribed hormones for almost two years; the Court awarded EUR 8,000 damages. Useful to this record: a trans visitor who is detained in Poland has a Europe-wide human-rights remedy against denial of HRT, though enforcement required litigation.

The page is anchored to Delta specifically: it records that in June 2018 Nigerian police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, on charges that they were gays and lesbians and that by July 2018 they were facing homosexuality-related charges in court, and that in August 2023 police raided a gay wedding in Warri, Delta state, arresting dozens in the case known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court following a mass arrest at a party or marriage ceremony. It also records nationwide patterns of arrests, raids and vigilante violence relevant to a traveller in Delta. This is the national-framework source for the record's claims that the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and that no state-specific protective statute exists.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note documents the national criminal framework that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and Section 217 of the Criminal Code making male gross indecency a felony liable to three years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states. It cites the USSD 2023 human rights report recording that on 27 August 2023 police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organized by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. It also quotes a human rights lawyer based in Warri, Delta state, on 'kito' (predatory same-sex assault) victims under-reporting for fear of prosecution. This confirms the national framework under which Delta stands and documents the recorded Delta-specific enforcement incidents underlying this record's position that state-level documentation is thin rather than demonstrating safety.

sources.title: Police arrest 67 gay suspects in Delta hotel - Daily Post Nigeria
sources.summary: Daily Post reports that police officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area of Delta State arrested 67 suspects on 27 August 2023 at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius (the groom), 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo (the bride), 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a male cross-dresser's confession that he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution, and that one suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. This is a direct, dated, on-the-ground record of enforcement action inside Delta State (Warri), evidencing that the national anti-LGBT framework is actively enforced in this jurisdiction and that incidents are frequently framed together with drug allegations.

27671186B95832466049157.name: Rivers
27671186B95832466049157.summary:
For a trans traveler Rivers carries no state-level protective statute: the national framework applies in full — a 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment, bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and reaches registering, operating or supporting gay organisations — and a foreign government's August 2026 travel advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation.

Practical safety in this state is documented directly: a 21-year-old gay man who travelled to this state in January 2015 to meet someone he had contacted on a social media platform was attacked and sexually abused there and did not report it to police; the national pattern after the 2014 statute includes arbitrary arrest and extortion by police, including 8 of 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday gathering in another state. A 2022 court ruling that certain sections of the 2014 statute are unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide did not remove the documented enforcement climate in practice, and the sources record no legal protections for LGBT+ people under the framework.

sources.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the SSMPA (passed January 2014) records that the law imposes 10 to 14 years' imprisonment on anyone who registers, operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. It documents that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the Act, including eight of the 21 young men arrested, but never charged, at a birthday party in Ibadan, and - relevant to Rivers State itself - the case of Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos who in January 2015 travelled to Port Harcourt to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there, saying he did not report it to the police. The named Port Harcourt incident and the nationwide abuse pattern substantiate the enforcement climate a same-sex couple or trans visitor faces in Rivers.

15666254B8535925993004.name: Sarawak
15666254B8535925993004.summary:
Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the national penal code with penalties up to 20 years' imprisonment and caning; legal gender recognition is unavailable, and a dual court system applies Sharia jurisdiction to Muslims only, so same-sex intimacy and 'cross-dressing' are criminalised for Muslims under religious-law enactments. No national law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported, with transgender people particularly vulnerable.

The enforcement pattern a visitor encounters is the national one: a 2022 human-rights report documents state religious authorities harassing LGBT activists and organisations and raiding private events across the parent nation, and the country-profile source records an anti-LGBT crackdown in progress since the 2018 election. The audited sources document no state/province-specific enforcement pattern; the national framework governs what a visitor encounters here.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under: as a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016) he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors' - the city ban enacted in 2012 that the cited New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered, with the page quoting his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when the pop diva visited the city. The page also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013. This is the most jurisdiction-specific enforcement origin available for the record's local assessment of LGBT-hostile measures in the city.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Russia) supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. The page records that ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and that Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia, SOGI (June 2025): same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023; the 2013 'gay propaganda' law is punishable by administrative fines (up to 400,000 rubles for individuals) or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment, and since the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2-6 years and organising 6-10 years' imprisonment (Article 282.2). Records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state able but not willing to provide protection. Region-specific: citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the note records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August on charges of participating in the activities of the 'extremist' 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature (Part 1 of Article 133) - the regional enforcement of the federal framework this record claims.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions (about 98 administrative, 3 criminal) for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation; between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Region-specific: in March, a Ulyanovsk-region doctor who faced a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the 'LGBT movement' and received a three-year sentence - the federal enforcement wave in operation inside this region, whose national score the record adopts.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. The national framework a visitor stands under is protective in form: the constitution bars sexual-orientation discrimination; after a 2005 judgment of the constitutional court, the elected national legislature legalised same-sex marriage in November 2006, so marriage-based partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse; and sex status can be changed in the population registry — and therefore on identity documents and passports — on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery (the 2003 alteration-of-sex-description law). The landmark ruling of 10 November 2025 in the trans-inmate case affirms gender-affirming healthcare as part of adequate medical care, although the case concerns a correctional facility in another division, so the national correctional policy is the correct frame for this division rather than any division-specific finding.

sources.summary: Court record (High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Medium B): the landmark ruling for a trans inmate against the Department of Correctional Services - refusal of gender expression (feminine attire, she/her pronouns), inadequate accommodation and denial of state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy held to be unfair discrimination; hormone therapy recognised as part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e).

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

19338628B73800214047876.name: Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes
19338628B73800214047876.summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score. The national framework a trans visitor stands under here: same-sex marriage and full adoption have been legal since 2013 (civil solidarity pacts since 1999); discrimination on gender identity is covered by the penal code since an 18 November 2016 amendment, with homophobic hate speech carrying fines up to EUR 45,000 and/or one year's imprisonment; legal gender recognition has required a court procedure rather than surgery, sterilisation or any medical intervention since 1 January 2017; and gender-affirming treatment is funded through the national health scheme with transsexualism classed as a long-term illness. Custodial exposure otherwise mirrors the national picture: placement follows the sex on identity documents and trans detainees suffer persistent serious rights violations, per the national prison-inspectorate (the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté).

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018), 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison': transgender women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal grey area and are punished for far more than their alleged crimes - first-person accounts of placement in an all-male facility (a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014, with detainee and staff hostility; an Argentinian trans woman's story of incarceration); Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees by the sex on their ID; the controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty says transgender detainees are the group that 'suffers the most' in prison; also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), unofficial English translation: official inspectorate opinion on the treatment of transgender persons in ALL places of deprivation of liberty; built on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station - eight trans women and one trans man interviewed); finds persistent serious violations of fundamental rights of trans detainees, isolation and overcrowding risks; recommends that the 2016 depathologising law (no more surgery requirement for civil-status change) be translated into prison regulations; explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

sources.summary: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

68945753B85747362819570.name: Gangwon
68945753B85747362819570.summary:
No province-specific law, ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans people is documented for Gangwon; the framework a visitor meets here is the national one: being trans is not criminalised, and the courts are steadily tightening what legal gender recognition may demand. A May 2024 ruling ended any surgical requirement for changing registered sex, and in July 2024 a court held that police telling a trans person to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed their rights, awarding damages after both instances found for the claimant, with an appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

For a visitor the operational reality is documented social friction around public restrooms, reported nationally rather than locally: Gangwon's audited record offers legality, functioning courts, no documented local hostility machinery, and no local facility-restriction law; restroom friction is a national-pattern finding, not a Gangwon one.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award (against a 3 million won claim), ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female - who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 - to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The article also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents (41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink, 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. This is the national framework this province is scored against; no KOR/Gangwon-specific incident appears.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria; the court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the framework this province is scored against; the wire contains no KOR/Gangwon-specific content.

68945753B85001375391280.name: Ulsan
68945753B85001375391280.summary:
No audited source documents any local law, ordinance or enforcement practice regarding trans people in this industrial city; the national framework applies undiminished: trans status is lawful; legal gender recognition is available without surgical prerequisites after a May 2024 ruling; and the July 2024 judgment holding that police advice to avoid public restrooms was a rights infringement — damages awarded, the appellate court declaring comfortable restroom access a fundamental and universal human right — binds police practice as elsewhere in the country. The same case file records a 2021 national survey of trans respondents showing widespread fear-driven avoidance of public facilities, and a 2021 damages award to a student barred from an academy's restrooms.

Within the audited record, nothing in this city's own conduct — administration, policing or incident history — either worsens or improves that national baseline. Its visitor-facing facts are therefore the framework plus the facility-avoidance survey, and no more.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award (against a 3 million won claim), ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female - who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020 - to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The article also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents (41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink, 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. This is the national framework this metropolitan city is scored against; no KOR/Ulsan-specific incident appears.

The ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the framework this metropolitan city is scored against; the wire contains no KOR/Ulsan-specific content.

1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
The Public Ministry's 2012–2021 study places La Libertad second in absolute LGTB-homicide count (10 of 88 — after Lima's 12, level with Lima Norte), centred on Trujillo. The region's population share (~3%) is far smaller than its death share (~11.4%), giving a per-capita lethality roughly 3.8× the national average — a materially concerning concentration not explained by population alone, and placing the unit below the national score (0.36).

Counterweight: Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (regional session 3 September 2024, approved 6 September 2024, published in El Peruano November 2024) promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people — their right to formal, dignified work in equitable conditions without discrimination on gender identity or expression, and recognition of the trans community as a vulnerable group. This is a resident-facing instrument (a visitor does not use it), but it evidences that this particular regional council legislated visibly for trans inclusion — the one such ordinance found in Peru's 26 departments. It also sits in the same department where rondas campesinas exercise recognised dispute-resolution authority, a structural caveat with no documented trans-specific case.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The per-capita violence concentration is the dominant factor; the ordinance prevents a larger deduction. vs Lima (now 0.38, above national): La Libertad's per-capita lethality remains worse, though Lima's higher absolute count and 2025 reporting case have lifted its score since the original comparison. vs Tacna (0.34): both are modestly below national, but La Libertad's multi-year dataset is more robust evidence than a single incident.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.

sources.summary: Wayka (27 May 2025): Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a hostel room in Tacna on 19 April 2025, the autopsy recording death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways, after entering the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone about two hours later; the case is being investigated as a possible hate crime - an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Context offered: Peru has no gender-identity-recognition legislation and no law sanctioning hate crimes, and activists note a recently promulgated legislative proposal (congressman Alejandro Muñante) restricting access to public bathrooms by sexual orientation; the Public Prosecutor's Office identified 84 criminal complaints on LGTB deaths between January 2012 and May 2021 (most victims gay men 55.8%, trans women 36.4%).

Trome (updated 21 May 2025): a 48-year-old trans woman was found dead inside the 'Los 5 Titos' hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna after entering on a Sunday with a man who later left alone carrying a white bag; she was initially processed as NN until identified through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage inside and outside the hostel to trace the suspect's escape route; relatives denounced the crime and demanded police action. The body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired; no suspect had been identified in the audited text.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
The rights organisation Caribe Afirmativo issues a specific, named warning of "increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the Atlántico department" in its 2025 annual report, and that escalation is the visitor-facing risk signal: the report designates Barranquilla, the department's main hub, and the nearby municipality of Soledad as areas at a "high" threat level, and names this department explicitly in the national victim total. The visitor-facing risk profile is public-space lethality, impunity and the named high-threat designation; the department's main hub is the centre of trans sex work and the city where the organisation's documentation base operates, giving a trans visitor elevated exposure in that hub.

A positive institutional signal is on record: the department's development plan, and the hub city's, commits coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violent acts against LGBTIQ+ people.

sources.summary: Publimetro Colombia (27 September 2026) on Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia': nationally 270 victims in 2025, a 63% increase over 2024 (165 homicides), one killing every 32 hours. For the Atlántico department it documents 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases, and designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories with 'high' threat levels for this population; it recalls the department's and Barranquilla's development plans commit coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people. It also reports threats show near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage.

Caribe Afirmativo's own 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia': in 2025 one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours, and violence runs a continuum from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity; the report documents territorial expansion of the violence, including towards territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and criticises the insufficient state response. The cached text does not break out Atlántico-specific counts (those are carried by the companion Publimetro piece); it underpins the national crisis-scale and territorial-expansion claims this record is scored against.

13589884B36646919284035.name: Caldas
13589884B36646919284035.summary:
No finding specific to Caldas on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources. The national reporting these sources carry frames what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country: an English-language international paper (April 2025) reported the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman beaten in daylight and filmed by onlookers in a metropolitan area elsewhere in the country, whose death from her injuries provoked national alarm over transfemicide; and an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in another part of the country circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women and forcing them from their homes, with dozens killed nationally.

Those reported cases concern other departments, in other parts of the country. Nothing here marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and because such violence surfaces where monitors and journalists can reach, the absence of Caldas-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.

sources.summary: El País English edition (14 April 2025) reports Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon with no one arrested; the article states hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. That national transfemicide alarm is the picture this department is assessed against; the report contains no Caldas-specific information.

The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women, quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide (recording the killings as ordinary cases), and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. This national armed-group violence and displacement baseline is what this department is assessed against; the report contains no Caldas-specific information.

13589884B23733272568917.name: Cundinamarca
13589884B23733272568917.summary:
No finding specific to Cundinamarca on law, enforcement practice or incidents for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources; the national framework these sources carry is what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country, and for this department the operative detail is documents. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a birth certificate — options include female, male and two further markers — and since August 2023 passports issued within the country offer three gender options; a 9 July 2026 decree obliges public notaries to complete a marker change within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free, and shields the change history from public disclosure, and a 4 February 2022 ruling by the national court ordered the further marker option to be offered to everyone. The process is a notarial one with no surgery or court ruling required, though a 2016 report documented some notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending psychiatric pathologisation.

The risk context reported elsewhere: an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in another part of the country circulating 'social cleansing' flyers naming trans women, giving them a week to leave, and killing more than forty trans women nationally in 2023; a further national report on the same pattern (August 2025) could not be retrieved in full at research time and is carried only as context; and a widely shared report of the killing of a trans woman in a metropolitan area elsewhere in the country prompted national alarm in April 2025 — that killing was reported in another department, not here.

Nothing in the record marks Cundinamarca as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and the absence of Cundinamarca-specific findings reflects where such violence gets reported, not proven safety.

On 9 July 2026 outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo signed Decree 0732 of 2026, which obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary ('NB') option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X). A 2016 report (Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS) documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Gender-marker change is a notarial/bureaucratic process with no surgery or court ruling required and applies equally in Cundinamarca.

The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary ('NB') option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X). Gender-marker change is a notarial/bureaucratic process with no surgery or court ruling required and applies equally in Cesar.

sources.summary: EL PAÍS English (14 Apr 2025) reports the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia: she was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April, and she died of a cardiac arrest that afternoon; police interrogated local residents but no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. 13589884B32024052187233.name: Huila
13589884B32024052187233.summary:
For a trans visitor to Huila the only department-specific legal item in the audited record is a protection outcome: in its 2000 ruling T-268 the constitutional court — the top of the national court system — permitted a gay pride parade in Neiva, the department's capital, after the mayor had prevented it, establishing constitutional protection for public expression of sexual orientation in Huila. Everything else a visitor faces is national: an August 2025 investigation documents a continuing wave of killings of queer and trans people — in parts of the country, being queer means "to sign your own death sentence" — and a 2024 report records armed groups circulating "social cleansing" threats against trans women, with 41 trans women killed nationally in 2023 and more killed that spring.

No Huila-specific statute, incident or enforcement mechanism beyond the 2000 ruling appears in the audited sources, and the national legal floor standing over the department — same-sex activity legal since 1981, orientation-based discrimination banned since 2011, same-sex marriage legal since April 2016, and legal gender change available since 1993 with birth-certificate markers F, M, NB and T — is the protection a visitor can actually rely on. What a visitor can plan on is the national pattern of high lethality and near-total impunity; nothing on this record marks Huila as better or worse than that baseline.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
Puno has no regional statute or incident of its own in the audited record, and the decisive facts are national, which means they apply in Puno like anywhere in the country. For a trans visitor the mechanism is legal rather than customary: a national measure approved by the legislature in 2025 bars trans people from using public restrooms corresponding to their gender identity, with narrow carve-outs for medical care, custody and accompanying minors or disabled persons and a ban on "ambiguous" restroom signage; its own trigger was a complaint about toilet signage at the capital's airport, and enforcement is expected to rest on security staff checking identity documents to decide who may use a women's restroom, so restroom access is the flashpoint the law itself creates. Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation.

A national human-rights institute published a detailed critique calling the measure institutionalised discrimination, and a leading activist notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. No local variation is documented for Puno, and no department-level enforcement or incident appears in the audited sources.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment (including ID checks), and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. It contains no Puno-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is the national ban on gender-matching restroom access that binds the region (committee stage, February 2025).

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) confirms that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It contains no Puno-specific finding; for this record its value is the human-rights institute's analysis of the national framework that governs the region.

1875124B82769317880582.name: Tumbes
1875124B82769317880582.summary:
Tumbes carries no regional law or incident entry in the audited record; what governs a trans visitor here is national. In 2025 the national legislature moved from committee unanimity in February to plenary approval in April (waiving a second vote) of a law prohibiting trans people from using public restrooms corresponding to their gender identity, with exceptions only for medical care, custody situations and accompanying children or disabled persons, and a leading human-rights institute's published analysis condemns it as legalised discrimination. Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation.

Because Tumbes is a border department, the practical note for a trans visitor is that the restroom rule — the very domain that triggered the law, via an airport-signage complaint — applies at public facilities including transport hubs, with no local mitigation documented for this department and enforcement expected to rest on staff checking identity documents at the door of a gendered restroom.

1875124B64829338827261.name: Piura
1875124B64829338827261.summary:
Piura has no statute, enforcement record or incident specific to trans visitors in the audited sources; the national framework is the whole of what is documented. For a trans visitor the mechanism is legal and countrywide: a 2025 national measure, whose own origin story is a complaint about restroom signage at the capital's airport, bars trans people from public restrooms corresponding to their gender identity — the law's own origin story indicates which everyday act it polices — with enforcement expected to rest on staff checking identity documents. Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation.

For a visitor this means the restroom statute is enforced countrywide: nothing marks Piura as an aggravation of, or refuge from, that national rule, and no local mitigation is documented for this department.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment (including ID checks), and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. It contains no Piura-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is the national ban on gender-matching restroom access that binds the region (committee stage, February 2025).

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) confirms that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It contains no Piura-specific finding; for this record its value is the human-rights institute's analysis of the national framework that governs the region.

1875124B61751373376494.name: Lambayeque
1875124B61751373376494.summary:
No trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern is documented for Lambayeque; the national framework applies in full. For a trans visitor the mechanism is legal: a 2025 national rule bars trans people from public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, medical care, accompanying under-12s, the elderly or disabled) and a ban on ambiguous restroom signage; enforcement would rest on individual staff checking identity documents, so restroom access depends on staff judgment. Legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation.

Violence risk is also national rather than department-specific: a university rights observatory recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases for 2020-2023, over half of them trans women (30 of 54), with 19 killings in 2023 alone, including an extortion-gang murder of a trans sex worker in February 2023; nothing marks Lambayeque as diverging from that baseline in either direction, and no local mitigation is documented for this department.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024), drawing on the annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia: Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023, the homicide victims being 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone (12 of them trans women), and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides (13 of 19 in 2023). The piece recounts the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots (Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier), with two killers arrested in March 2023, and notes the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. This is the national violence baseline this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

1875124B15182629165166.summary:
For Ancash no trans-specific regional law, ordinance or incident series is documented; every available source is national, and the national framework governs the visitor: a measure barring trans people from public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, medical care, accompanying children under 12, the elderly or disabled) and a ban on ambiguous restroom signage, was enacted as national law (32331) on 13 May 2025 per the freshness record, which marks the earlier legislative-movement coverage as superseded by the enacted law. Enforcement would rest on individual staff checking identity documents, and legal gender recognition remains long, costly and invasive, so identity documents frequently do not match a trans person's presentation.

Violence risk is also national rather than department-specific: a university observatory recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights violations for 2020-2023 (30 trans women), including a 2023 extortion-gang murder of a trans sex worker; nothing marks Ancash as deviating in either direction, and no local mitigation is documented for this department.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Ancash-specific content.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Ancash-specific content.

Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024), drawing on the annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia: Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023, the homicide victims being 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone (12 of them trans women), and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides (13 of 19 in 2023). The piece recounts the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots (Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier), with two killers arrested in March 2023, and notes the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. This is the national violence baseline this department is scored against; the article contains no Ancash-specific content.

blindSourceSummaries: A digital news outlet (February 2025): the legislature's women's and family committee unanimously approved a package of two 2023 bills that would prohibit entry to public restrooms designated for the sex assigned at birth (exceptions: custody, medical attention, accompanying a person under 12, an elderly or disabled person) and prohibit ambiguous bathroom signage; the package still required a plenary vote. An activist notes no official statistics on trans violence in public restrooms exist, and enforcement would rest on individual security staff checking identity documents.

A university human-rights institute's bulletin (April 2025): in early April 2025 the legislature's plenary approved, waiving a second vote, a law strengthening protection of children and adolescents against sexual violations (merging two 2023 bills). A provision of the bill bans entry to and use of public restrooms for any person whose biological sex does not match the facility's designated sex, with narrow exceptions for accompaniment or assistance and legal or judicial mandates. The bulletin reads the provision as a direct violation of equality and non-discrimination (the constitution's equality clause and a regional human-rights convention, in line with the regional human-rights court's advisory opinion), and as validating stereotypes about trans people.

An LGBTI news outlet (July 2024) on the annual report of a university LGBTI rights observatory: 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; more than half the homicide victims were trans women (30), then gay men (23) and one lesbian woman; yearly homicides 2020: 12 (8 trans women), 2021: 10, 2022: 13, 2023: 19 (12 trans women). Killings involved extreme cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabblings, throat-cuttings); rights violations peaked at 61 in 2020 (43 in 2022, 34 in 2023, 32 in 2021), trans women again the most affected. Includes testimony that in February 2023 an extortion gang abducted a 31-year-old sex worker in the capital's central area and killed her in a district on the outskirts with about 30 shots, a case of the sex-trade organised-crime violence the movement identifies as the main trans-femicide driver.

1875124B63771233756824.name: Apurímac
1875124B63771233756824.summary:
No documented sub-national signal exists for Apurímac: the country dossier lists this department among the regions where no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding could be located, and all three attached sources are national in scope. The operative legal fact for a visitor is the national frame: a congressional package (bills 6506 and 8457, committee-approved February 2025) barring people from public sanitary facilities designated for the opposite sex at birth — with exceptions only for custody, medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities — was approved by the plenary on 2 April 2025 and enacted as Law 32331 on 13 May 2025, so a trans traveler now faces a live national legal exposure when using public restrooms.

Practical safety: national data record 54 killings of TLGBI people between 2020 and 2023, with trans women most affected (30 of the homicide victims) and hate crimes rising (19 in 2023, up from 13 in 2022); no regional deviation is documented either way.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment (including ID checks), and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. It contains no Apurímac-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is the national ban on gender-matching restroom access that binds the region (committee stage, February 2025).

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) confirms that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It contains no Apurímac-specific finding; for this record its value is the human-rights institute's analysis of the national framework that governs the region.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024), covering the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabbings), and the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination (61 denuncias in 2020). It recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. It contains no Apurímac-specific finding; for this record its value is the national hate-violence data the regional assessment relies on.

IDEHPUCP analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) reports the Congress plenary on 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from second vote, the dictamen of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes', whose article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying/assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The authors argue the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; they note Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage. No Arequipa-specific finding appears; the source supports this record's critique claim.

25984515B95172477822815.name: Adana
25984515B95172477822815.summary:
Adana has no province-specific law, ordinance or incident series in the audited record; a trans visitor here stands under the same national framework that binds every province. A leaked October 2025 draft omnibus justice package (the '11th Judicial Package') would enable criminal charges against LGBT people nationwide, and it contains no province-specific provisions; if adopted it would apply to this province unchanged.

Legal protections for a visitor: same-sex sexual activity has been legal since an Ottoman-era penal code (1858), and trans people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 — the document-relevant pathway — but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition, so marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are all unavailable and a partner has no spousal legal standing when travelling together. The LGBTI association Kaos GL reported that in 2025 anti-LGBTI hostility became institutionalised as a national policy line under a 'Year of the Family' campaign centered on the family, with senior officials' rhetoric and instructions to public institutions creating a climate encouraging rights violations — the practical-safety context a visitor encounters.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Kırıkkale included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness making members unfit for service, and conscripts who declare their homosexuality have to provide photographic proof. Same-sex marriage is not recognised; a 2012 constitutional-writing request to include it was rejected by both the AKP and the MHP. Authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years and police have used tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans; on 14 June 2019 the 7th Izmir Pride, the 3rd Antalya Pride and the 27th Istanbul Pride were banned by the cities' governors. The page also records a February 2026 newspaper report that the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex', with a sentence of one to three years in prison.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBTQ rights in Turkey' page is the framework a trans visitor in Kütahya stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the military, and same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised. Pride parades have been banned by local authorities since 2015 (Istanbul's 2015-2018 parades were banned and dispersed). The 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 dropped provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, though these carry no legal marital status; in early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', which was ultimately not included in that year's package, and in September 2026 police detained dozens in raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists under a 'Decade of Family and Population' crackdown.

sources.title: Human rights in Türkiye - Amnesty International
sources.summary: Amnesty International's 'Human rights in Türkiye' report (2025) documents the national framework that applies to Kütahya: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - which would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

An online encyclopedia's national page is the framework a trans visitor in this province stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the 1858 penal code, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page, the national framework that governs Sakarya (a Marmara-region province where national law applies): homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858, and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40 with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital. sources.title: Factsheet on leaked law proposals against LGBTI+ rights in Türkiye - Amnesty International
sources.summary: Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet analyses the leaked '11th Judicial Package', a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, Civil Code and six other laws that was leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025. It is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The draft would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 and add further conditions; Amnesty warns it would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are nationwide proposals that would apply within every province including Sakarya, whose record already notes the leaked October 2025 package.
