19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law alongside the national femicide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. For a trans visitor, the operative risk is police identification and detention: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident.

sources.summary: National-scope report (Washington Blade, Apr 10, 2025) on the national framework this city sits under: the administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law (which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs), and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Blade that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

National hate-crime observatory data for 2025 (Agencia Presentes, 19 Mar 2026) — the national monitoring record this city sits under: at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record at one crime every 38 hours. 32% of crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases); most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

National-framework source: via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty — inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere — prohibiting those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Direction: worse than national — the only Brazilian state in the country to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and the venue of a nationally decisive refusal. A trans woman was refused entry to the women's bathroom by staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre, urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to take public transport home; on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving these refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules — the legal exposure a visibly trans visitor faces using bathrooms in shops, restaurants and transport hubs.

In the other direction, the state has a visible LGBTQ tourism scene with pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages and marker changes, and nationwide legal rights are identical, so visitors see the same national protections as elsewhere.

sources.summary: Encyclopaedic national-rights page containing Santa Catarina-specific entries: the state's constitution (anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002) lists sexual orientation among non-discrimination grounds but, as of 2019, does not address discrimination against transgender people; from 2020 people in Santa Catarina obtain documents recording non-binary gender judicially or through notarial offices even though no specific law prescribes it; in Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. National framework claimed by the record: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013 (CNJ Resolution 175/2013) and the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling making discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation/gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Outright International country page: constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions following the 2019 Supreme Court ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, yet a deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee (a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019) for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy, and the Superior Court of Justice ruled nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity. 13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia contains the city at the centre of the country's most alarming recent record on anti-trans killings. On 4 April 2025 in Bello, a 32-year-old trans woman, Sara Millerey González Borja, was beaten and thrown into a waterway while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries. She was the third LGBT person killed in Bello that year — the first two were gay men — and the case triggered vigils, protests in several cities and a presidential order to investigate.

For a trans visitor the operative risk is lethal violence concentrated in this department's metro area: the surviving record supports a lethal concentration — three municipal killings within four months — and documents no department-level protection machinery specific to it.

sources.summary: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups circulating in Caquetá - where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement - distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there were forced to flee after death threats. Retained per rule 5: this supports the record's national-frame claims (2023-24 kill tallies and the southern-department social-cleansing flyers) and no region-specific Antioquia source covers them.

19338628B30439183828151.name: Bourgogne-Franche-Comté
19338628B30439183828151.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Dijon / Cote-d'Or: rural traditional department. Regional evidence: the only prefecture in the country found to have twice banned a Pride march from its city centre with the ban upheld - on 12 June 2025 the prefecture prohibited the Pride 2025 march in central Dijon citing "risk of trouble to public order", the second consecutive year of the same restriction; the organisers' withdrawal citing LGBT visibility was itself called significant by the city. On 14 June 2025 the administrative court rejected the legal challenge, and the march (about 1,500 people per police) proceeded on a diverted route around the historic centre; the prefecture justified the ban by estimated organiser numbers (200 vs previous 2,500 and 1,500 turnouts) and a stated risk of violent individuals attaching themselves. The march itself passed peacefully ("joyful and festive, without a hitch") - the harm documented here is the restriction and its chilling effect, not violence. Scored relative to the national score (0.67) for France.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
The region's documented contact point with trans-visitor risk is prison placement, which national law sets: under criminal-procedure code Article D248 a trans prisoner is held according to the sex on their identity documents, so trans women still marked male are placed in all-male facilities. An investigation published in January 2018 recorded exactly that near the region's principal city: Paola, shouted at and threatened by inmates during three days in a men's facility after a 2014 transfer, and — in the capital — Kara B., held under notorious conditions after a 2016 protest trial; the national detention inspector-general calls transgender detainees the group that suffers most in custody.

The inspector-general's May 2021 opinion, covering every place of deprivation of liberty in the state and built from some forty referrals since 2010, finds serious violations persisting: isolation by reason of trans status, untrained staff, and a 2016 depathologisation law never translated into prison rules. It recommends that detainees choose the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation and trans-only wings, and requires continuity of hormone and medical care — recommendations whose non-implementation is itself part of the documented picture for visitors who are detained anywhere in the state, including here.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

65028918B14696209246677.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
65028918B14696209246677.summary: Region research direction: mixed — the country's largest LGBTQ+ community and its biggest police raids coexist, with police acting without legal basis. (1) 1 February 2025: police arrested 56 men at a hotel in the capital at a reported "gay sex party"; organisers risk pornography-law prosecution with penalties up to 15 years; Amnesty International Indonesia called the police's "discriminatory and senseless harassment of LGBTI people ... has no basis in law" and demanded release of those detained. (2) One of the eight provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations — and simultaneously the city with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices; an assessor should expect both to be true at once. National climate from this record's sources: an October 2025 presidential decree listed "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among the country's non-military national security threats alongside terrorism and drugs, amplifying self-censorship (editors killing LGBTQ+ stories for fear of state reprisal); police deny violence and extortions in the 2022 death-in-custody of a US-based trans activist arrested on drug charges at Bali airport while family members allege he was beaten. Model-estimate residual (route 3, best-knowledge delta): sheer scale of the community limits enforcement reach.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Indonesia' page supplies the national framework the capital stands under and documents Jakarta's raid pattern in detail: police arrested 141 people over a 'gay sex party' in Jakarta in May 2017, detained 144 at the Atlantis Gym sauna on 21 May 2017 (ten charged), and arrested 51 at a Central Jakarta sauna in October 2017 (six charged), all pursued under the pornography law. More recently it records 56 people detained at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine detained at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 arrested at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025 — offences there can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'. Transgender people may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval, and there is no general anti-discrimination law, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific statute.

Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa raid 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that 'exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia', and demanded the release of those arrested. The release notes that police made the arrests without naming detainees or conducting judicial proceedings, and that those detained risk up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

The capital is one of a small set of provinces where an international NGO found discriminatory regional regulations — and simultaneously the place with the country's densest LGBTQ+ infrastructure, media presence and monitoring-group offices; an assessor should expect both to be true at once. The organisation's local deputy director called the villa raid 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that 'exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in the country', and demanded the release of those arrested. 1811400B15614733245507.name: Mahārāshtra
1811400B15614733245507.summary: Region research direction: worse than national on public-festival access screening — religion-based identity verification doubles as an outing mechanism for gender-nonconforming visitors. After the VHP publicly urged garba (autumn dance festival) organisers not to allow non-Hindus and to check Aadhaar cards for entry, a political row erupted; in Nagpur organisers imposed Aadhaar verification, security checks with "male and female" boundaries and a ritual bow before a Varaha avatar as entry conditions. An identity-checked, religion-screened entry gate at a public festival is precisely the mechanism by which a gender-nonconforming visitor is examined and outed by authorities who are not supposed to be involved — and it is happening in named cities, not nationwide. National backdrop from this record's sources: parliament passed a 2026 amendment bill removing the right to self-identify, limiting recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification for gender-affirming procedures, and creating offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender punishable with up to life in prison — prompting nationwide protests from trans communities, with a Supreme Court-appointed panel asking the government to withdraw it; the national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards needed for social security.

sources.summary: National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026, on the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, which the record's national-backdrop paragraph relies on: the bill amends the 2019 law, removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of "coercing or alluring" a person to be transgender that HRW calls reminiscent of colonial-era provisions criminalising transgender persons for appearing dressed as women; India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security. No Maharashtra-specific content in this source (the record's Nagpur entry-screening claim is not covered here); the article supports the record's claim that this national framework applies in every state including Maharashtra.

National-framework BBC News article on the same 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now needing presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify, limiting recognition, in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court "third gender"/self-determination ruling; critics warn it could exclude many transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from welfare benefits, and lawyer N Kavitha Rameshwar called the medical-certification requirement an "attack on the privacy and dignity of the individual", while the government argues the narrower definition targets those facing "extreme and oppressive" discrimination and prevents exploitation and trafficking. No Maharashtra-specific content (the record's Nagpur/VHP/Aadhaar festival-screening claim is not covered by this source); the article supports the record's national-backdrop claims.

1811400B23625213884851.name: Delhi
1811400B23625213884851.summary:
Delhi sits at the centre of the country's 2026 reversal on trans rights: parliament passed an amendment bill removing the right to self-identification, restricting legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandating medical certification, and creating new offences of coercion and allurement punishable up to life imprisonment — a de facto reversal of the 2014 constitutional self-determination ruling, cleared by both houses and awaiting presidential assent. The bill triggered rallies in the capital in March 2026, and a supreme-court-appointed advisory panel urged its withdrawal amid privacy and dignity challenges.

The capital is also where the country's trans population is most institutionally visible: the most recent national census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 held identity documents — the documentation gap and the protest politics both concentrate here.

sources.summary: National-framework HRW news release, 26 March 2026 — core source for the record's claims: the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates "coercing or alluring" offences that could criminalise support systems; HRW calls it a major reversal of hard-won rights and urges the president not to sign it. India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons but only about 32,500 hold the identity cards essential for social security — the national documentation gap the record concentrates in the capital. No Delhi-specific event in this source.

National-framework BBC News article on the 2026 amendment bill: approved by both houses and now awaiting presidential assent; it removes the right to self-identify in a reversal of the 2014 Supreme Court ruling; the record's capital-protest-politics claim is evidenced here — activist Grace Banu told a press conference in Delhi the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation" — and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider amid privacy-and-dignity challenges. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protections against exploitation and trafficking.

68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary:
The capital's courts have been the country's clearest rights forum for trans people: a ruling finalised in July 2024 held that police who told a transgender person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while had infringed personal rights, calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right and awarding damages. A 2021 district-court judgment likewise awarded damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

Practical safety rests in part on national data a visitor shares in public facilities: a 2021 survey of 591 trans respondents found 41% had used a restroom of another gender out of fear of mistreatment, 39% restricted food and drink to avoid public restrooms, and 36% went without. On recognition and documents, gender-marker change has liberalised judicially: a May 2024 regional decision approved marker change for five trans people without surgery, holding that a surgery requirement violates bodily integrity and reducing the old surgical prerequisites to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them.

sources.summary: Seoul-specific ruling coverage (Korea Times, 22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court (presiding judge Chung In-jae) dismissed the state's appeal and ruled partially for plaintiff A in a damages lawsuit against the state, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed; the decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed, holding that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights — "the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right." Underpinning data: a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether; the piece also cites a 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling of 7 million won damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to one's gender identity; the national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The ruling is not from a capital court — it evidences the national judicial trend the record cites for Seoul, and no Seoul-specific source covers that claim.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Worse than national for what a visitor actually meets: this is the main tourist corridor, a large international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but police forces at both municipal and state level have repeatedly been documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people. Multiple recorded assaults during detention are concentrated in the two most visited resort towns; officers are described as untrained in human-rights standards; the municipal diversity office recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman; and two tourist-police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals.

Documents and screening: the airport city's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — directly relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Useful legal counterweights are resident-facing, and the record is scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch feature (31 March 2025), 'Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges'. Country-wide survey of legal gender recognition: 22 of 32 states had legislated an LGR procedure by March 2025, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco, Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans people's documents permanently mismatched; also documents coercive detention and border scrutiny risks for document-mismatched travellers.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mexico - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Mexico' page gives the state-level legal picture a Quintana Roo visitor stands under: same-sex marriage has been permitted in the state since 2012 (two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 once the state conceded its Civil Code sets no gender requirement), and the state congress legalized adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022. The page records Quintana Roo among the states that enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and that banned conversion practices on 15 December 2023, and lists the Quintana Roo penal code among hate-crime laws punishing crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender. It also notes the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination and that Cancún is among Mexico's principal gay-tourism destinations.

sources.title: Quintana Roo y Morelos prohíben las terapias de conversión - Tribuna de la Bahía
sources.summary: Local reporting (Tribuna de la Bahía, 15 December 2023) on the Quintana Roo congress joining Morelos in banning conversion practices: both legislatures approved initiatives prohibiting and sanctioning 'Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual e Identidad de Género' (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA (measurement and updating unit) value for those who carry out such practices. This pins the December 2023 reform to a concrete date and gives the sanction levels in force across the state, including tourist corridors such as Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary:
This state is where the country's religious-enforcement apparatus has been most visibly exercised against gender expression: in 2021 its religious department issued an arrest warrant for a prominent transgender businesswoman over her presentation and mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers in a manhunt that preceded her leaving the country, an episode documented in international analysis of state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia.

The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct is criminalised with sentences up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and the day-to-day exposure for gender-nonconforming visitors runs precisely through this state's religious-offence enforcement.

sources.summary: Malaysia country profile (Human Dignity Trust, last updated 16 December 2025) with both the national framework and Selangor-specific enforcement: Penal Code sections 377A-377D criminalise same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment with whipping (a law enforced in recent years; both men and women, and usable against trans people), and Sharia state enactments criminalise cross-dressing and "males posing as females"; Selangor-specific content — the Federal Court struck down provisions of Selangor's Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 as exceeding state power (2021), the Selangor state authorities issued an arrest warrant for a trans businesswoman who failed to appear in court and announced the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers (the Sajat case), and a Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six to seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane; at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on the LGBT community ongoing since the 2018 election.

HRW/Justice for Sisters report release (10 August 2022) documenting Malaysia's state-backed discrimination, including the Selangor episode the record leads with: in 2021 Nur Sajat, a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur, failed to appear in court in Selangor to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" based on her attire; the state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, then sought her extradition from Thailand — a deployment HRW/JFS cite as showing how far authorities go to enforce rigid gender norms (she was permitted to stay under UNHCR protection and later settled in Australia). 15666254B42356713390762.name: Johor
15666254B42356713390762.summary:
No protective or tolerant regime specific to this state is on record: a visitor's exposure is the national baseline, enforced locally. Same-sex conduct is criminalised with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and public-morality offences are enforced through the state's religious authorities — the channel international monitoring documents as driving state-backed discrimination against LGBT people; state religious law separately criminalises cross-dressing and same-sex intimacy for Muslims.

The one documented local divergence beyond that baseline is adverse: in November 2023 the state government announced plans to establish 'conversion-therapy centres' to rehabilitate LGBT people.

sources.summary: National-framework source (applies country-wide, including the state of Malacca): the Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile (last updated 2024) reports the Federal Penal Code 1936 ss.377A/377B criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years’ imprisonment and whipping, and s.377D “outrages on decency” criminalises gross indecency in terms that can be used to target transgender people; state Sharia enactments additionally criminalise “cross-dressing” for Muslims. It records evidence of the law being enforced in recent years, a crackdown on the LGBT community since the 2018 election, a high-profile 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman fleeing the country following threats of arrest, and consistent reports of discrimination and violence with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Malacca-specific breakdown): HRW report (published 10 Aug 2022 with Justice for Sisters) documents government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia, citing the federal penal code punishing oral and anal sex with up to 20 years in prison and Sharia law codes in the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya that typically criminalise same-sex activity and gender nonconformity. It details a hostile official climate — “rehabilitation” and conversion programs, officials shutting down events, and the 2021 prosecution of transgender woman Nur Sajat in western Selangor — and concludes pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity influences law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behavior, and public discourse.

27671186B76269877687363.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Worse than national: the territory's most publicly visible trans person was killed on 8 August 2024 — found beaten and bruised beside a main highway hours after posting a routine video, having previously expressed fear for her life — and police have not charged anyone. A human-rights group has sued the federal government and the police for failing to investigate, seeking a court order to compel investigation and prosecution after multiple petitions were ignored, which qualifies the killing under a test of official failure rather than leaving it a lone incident. Reporting on the capital's queer scene documents threats and raids alongside informal community organising.

The national framework applies here unchanged for a visitor: a 2014 act reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalises same-sex conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment, extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and to activities of gay groups and organisations; dating-app gangs are a documented extortion pattern country-wide; and a foreign government's travel advisory (August 2026) warned LGBT travellers of arrest, violence, attacks and blackmail risks. Scored relative to the national score (0.08).

sources.summary: Region-specific: BBC News (article dated 9 Aug 2024) reports the beaten, bruised body of 33-year-old transgender TikToker “Abuja Area Mama” was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life; a police statement described the victim as “a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification”. Abuja police chief Benneth Igweh ordered a “thorough and discreet” investigation, and the article notes that although Nigerian laws guarantee freedom from discrimination, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states.

Region-specific: The Dial (Issue 25) reports police found Area Mama dead on an Abuja highway hours after her last video; Abuja police’s preliminary statement described her as “a man fully dressed in female clothing”, and six months later no suspects had been charged despite a promised “thorough and discreet” investigation. It details the legal floor her killers faced — the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforcing colonial-era laws criminalising same-sex activity as “carnal knowledge against the order of nature” punishable by up to 14 years’ imprisonment, bans on same-sex marriage and civil unions, gay organisations and public LGBTQ+ expression, death-by-stoning risk under northern Sharia law, no legal route to change gender, and cross-dressing bans under Sharia in the north and in the Nigerian military — and records a nearly 6,000-signature petition demanding investigation of her murder as a hate crime.

National-framework source (applies country-wide; no Abuja-specific breakdown): Sahara Reporters (19 Aug 2026) reports the United Kingdom's foreign office warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of the risk of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation. The advisory states same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract lengthy prison sentences, that some northern states operating under Sharia law can impose the death penalty, and that the law also extends to people who help arrange or conduct same-sex marriages and criminalises activities involving gay groups and organisations; breaching curfews or movement restrictions could expose travellers to arrest and detention.

1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary:
Lima concentrates the country's sharpest documented lethal risk and its newest legal restriction. A national observatory counted 54 LGBTI+ murders for 2020–2023, with trans women the most affected (30 of the dead), amid rising hate crimes in which no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings.

In 2025 the national congress — sitting in the capital — approved a norm barring trans people from public bathrooms of a sex not matching their birth sex (committee vote February 2025, plenary approval April 2025), with the text also barring 'ambiguous' bathroom signage of the kind the capital's international airport had installed. A national human-rights institute analysed the norm as legalised discrimination with direct consequences for access to public space, and enforcement is expected to rest on security staff's judgment of whether an entering woman is trans. For a trans visitor, the capital is where both mechanisms bite: the bathroom-restriction norm is national policy administered here, and the murder pattern shows the violence exposure when prosecutions are rare and official statistics thin.

sources.summary: National-framework source (binds Lima as national policy): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the Muñante initiative barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth, stating the text also bars “ambiguous” bathroom signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”) and that the norm still required plenary backing. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and describing how enforcement would reduce to security staff demanding ID (DNI) based on their own judgment of whether a woman entering is trans.

National-framework source (the norm is national policy, enacted by the congress that sits and operates in Lima): IDEHPUCP analysis (15 Apr 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte) reports the Congress plenary on Wednesday 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from a second vote, the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR; article 5 of the text prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, with listed exceptions. The authors call the rule direct legislation that conditions basic rights on a “biological sex”, a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note trans people, though framed as aggressors, are more often victims of violence and discrimination.

National-framework source (observatory counts include Lima): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023, more than half of the dead being trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; 2023 saw the most homicides (19) and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. It recounts the 12 Feb 2023 kidnapping of transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the “Los Gallegos” extortion gang, who killed her with roughly 30 gunshots, and flags state inaction: no official system records victims’ sexual orientation and hate crimes go unsanctioned.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara is the administrative core of what the country's leading LGBTI rights organisation — reporting from its capital launch event in 2025 — documented as hostility turned into explicit state policy: presidency-centred targeting, the family ministry as implementing body, broadcast and platform censorship, an LGBTI organisation closed, six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated) with trans people most affected, and no official hate-crime statistics in existence. A leaked October 2025 judicial package would add up to three years' imprisonment for conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion, and bar gender-affirming care below age 25.

The capital hosts the machinery that drafts and enforces those measures; nothing on record shows local countervailing protection, and the same courts and ministries that field the report operate here.

sources.summary: National-framework source (applies country-wide; the package is drafted and enforced by institutions operating in Ankara): HRW (29 Oct 2025) reports the leaked draft “11th Judicial Package” would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years’ prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

National-framework monitoring report (the institutions it names — the presidency, the Ministry of Family — operate in Ankara): Kaos GL’s annual report (“The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People”, launched in 2025) finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy — hostility centered on the presidency, the Ministry of Family as implementing ministry, broadcasts censored and artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. It documents six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected, a sharp rise in torture and ill-treatment violations (89 versus 51 the previous year), and notes the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a leaked '11th Judicial Package' would amend the penal and civil codes with articles threatening LGBT people — behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion' (up to three years' prison, amending the indecent-acts provision); sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility); potential charges against trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists; justified as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Eskişehir stands, and it names the province directly: in June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. It also records that Kadir Has University surveys saw public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rise from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

sources.title: Turkish police attack Eskişehir's first planned Pride march, detain 20 - Duvar English
sources.summary: Duvar English reports that days after police interventions in Istanbul and Ankara, Turkish police attacked Eskişehir's first planned Pride march: officers were on the scene hours before the scheduled meeting time conducting identity checks, organisers were not allowed to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of 'violating the ban on the march'. The article notes Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years citing security concerns and public order. This is direct, locally specific evidence of how the national Pride-ban policy was enforced in Eskişehir itself, the key factual basis for this record's risk assessment.

Mülteci-Der's report on Syrian trans women living here found they cannot find work, face exploitation and harassment when they do, and have 'no faith in justice'. National frame: the leaked October 2025 draft would criminalise 'conduct contrary to biological sex' and its promotion (up to 3 years) and restrict gender-affirming care (minimum age 25); a 2025 rights report records hostility as explicit state policy, six violations of the right to life, trans people most affected. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reports a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus '11th Judicial Package' (national framework; the record's national-frame claim on the draft rests on this) that would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would amend civil code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing deemed-illegal interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison and trans people receiving such care up to three years, with courts able to order pretrial detention; fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and HRW warns it would force treatment into unregulated underground settings.

Kaos GL's report on 2025 ('A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy'; national framework, backing the record's national-frame claims) finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy: for the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy. It documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations, and 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025 — roughly two and a half times the previous year — citing detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants as main reasons.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (nav-only cache); the underlying news report covers 31 July 2025 mass ID roundups of trans women in a large-city entertainment district — names recorded, videos taken, no official reason given.
